condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.2 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Intonation can signal that a declarative is being used as a question without changing its syntactic clause type.

correct.text: Is the library open?
Which desk should I use?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Polar questions and the polarity of answers
statement: A polar question defines a positive answer and its negative counterpart. Yes and no track the polarity of the answer in the illustrated English pattern.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.3 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: A bare yes may be disfavored after a negative question. Fragments and declaratives can also express polar questions.

correct.text: Is the printer working? — No, it isn't.
Isn't the printer working? — Yes, it is.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Polar questions and the polarity of answers
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Answer sets and form of alternative questions
statement: An alternative question presents its candidate answers through or-coordination. Spoken alternatives commonly show rising pitch on an earlier coordinate and falling pitch on the last.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.4 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The coordinates can be phrases or clauses, and there can be more than two.

correct.text: Would you like soup, salad, or noodles?
Are we meeting inside or outside?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Answer sets and form of alternative questions
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Polar and alternative readings of or
statement: An or sequence can offer alternative answers or form a single proposition whose truth is at issue. Either paired with or forces the latter reading in the construction described here.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.4 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The first question can be ambiguous in writing. Spoken prosody and context can disambiguate.

correct.text: Are you free on Monday or Friday?
Are you free on either Monday or Friday?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Polar and alternative readings of or
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Alternative question meaning comes from coordination. The clauses involved may have the same form as clauses expressing polar questions.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.4 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Whether can appear in both coordinates in an embedded alternative question.

correct.text: Did Saira call or did Leon text?
I can't tell whether the switch is broken or whether the bulb has failed.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A polar-alternative question explicitly coordinates a proposition with its negative counterpart. A polar question expresses one proposition and derives its opposite.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.4 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Ellipsis can reduce the second coordinate. In embedded questions or not may immediately follow whether.

correct.text: Is the cabinet locked or not?
Is the cabinet locked?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Licensing of alternatives in embedded and exhaustive constructions
statement: In the illustrated frames, wonder licenses polar and alternative complements, whereas doubt takes the polar pattern. The exhaustive conditional requires an alternative reading.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.4 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The restriction concerns interpretation. An or inside a polar complement does not necessarily make that complement an alternative question.

correct.text: I wonder whether the latch is open or closed.
I'll start whether the latch is open or not.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Licensing of alternatives in embedded and exhaustive constructions
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Pragmatic differences between polar and polar-alternative questions
statement: The explicit negative in a polar-alternative question can emphasize choice or exhaustiveness. Ordinary polar wording can better fit a speaker already inclined toward one answer.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.4 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Insistence is a contextual effect rather than an invariant meaning of or not.

correct.text: Have you paid the invoice?
Have you paid the invoice or not?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Pragmatic differences between polar and polar-alternative questions
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A variable question defines an answer by asking for a value for an interrogative variable. The question can specify a limited range of values.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.5 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: An explicitly limited set of values still permits a variable question.

correct.text: Who unlocked the cabinet?
Which of the two keys unlocked it?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A main open interrogative can keep a non-subject interrogative phrase in its ordinary postverbal position without inversion. This occurs in some sustained inquiries.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.5 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: An in-situ question can ask for new information rather than repeat or clarify prior speech.

correct.text: And you signed the form where?
You received how many invoices, exactly?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Infinitival open interrogatives in these constructions have no overt subject. To-infinitivals occur in headings and in some independent questions, while bare infinitivals occur mainly with why.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.5 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Independent to-infinitival questions can be literary. Bare how examples are marginal. Why not plus a plain verb commonly conveys a suggestion.

correct.text: How to repair a loose hinge
Why replace the whole cabinet?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Number and coordination of question variables
statement: An open question can ask for several values at once. Coordinated interrogative phrases can share a grammatical function or express different functions.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.5 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Values for coordinated phrases need not themselves be coordinated when the phrases express different functions.

correct.text: How many coats and how many blankets should we bring?
When and where will the meeting take place?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Number and coordination of question variables
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Single fronting of uncoordinated interrogative phrases
statement: In the illustrated multi-variable questions, at most one of the uncoordinated interrogative phrases is fronted.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.5 of Chapter 10.
violation: Two distinct uncoordinated interrogative phrases are fronted in the same finite open question.

exceptions.description: Preserve coordination, single complex interrogative phrases, in-situ interrogatives, and separate clauses.

correct.text: What did she hand to whom?
Where did they store which boxes?

incorrect.text: What to whom did she hand?
Where which boxes did they store?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Single fronting of uncoordinated interrogative phrases
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

diagnostic.error_pattern: Two distinct uncoordinated interrogative phrases are fronted in the same finite open question.
minimal_pairs: What to whom did she hand? ||| What did she hand to whom?
Where which boxes did they store? ||| Where did they store which boxes?
diagnostic.learner_explanation: In the illustrated multi-variable questions, at most one of the uncoordinated interrogative phrases is fronted.
diagnostic.corrected_paragraph_template: Front one question phrase and leave the other in its ordinary position.
false_positive_guards: When and where will they meet?
Which of these boxes did they store?
She handed what to whom?

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Values and pairing in multi-variable answers
statement: A singulary answer supplies one value per variable. A multiple answer supplies tuples. In a multi-variable question, how values are paired can form part of the answer.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.5 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: A single-variable question can receive an elaborated response that goes beyond its answer requirements.

correct.text: Who delivered what? — Ira delivered the maps.
Who delivered what? — Ira delivered the maps and Cora delivered the labels.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Values and pairing in multi-variable answers
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Juxtaposed variable and polar or alternative questions
statement: A variable question can be followed by a polar or alternative question that proposes a value or narrows the available values.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.5 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Apparent coordination in a reduced continuation need not represent coordination inside the first interrogative clause.

correct.text: Where did Jo leave it? In the car?
Who called? Ben or Sal?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Juxtaposed variable and polar or alternative questions
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Answers to information questions characteristically make statements. Answers to direction questions characteristically tell the questioner what to do. Both uses occur across polar, alternative, and variable questions.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.6 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Yes and no can serve in both answer patterns. A directive cannot be evaluated as true or false in the way a statement can.

correct.text: Did I shut the door? — Yes, you did.
Shall I shut the door? — Yes, shut it.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Shall and should in direction questions
statement: First-person main questions with shall can ask for direction. Some questions with shall or should also have a predictive or epistemic reading in an appropriate context.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.6 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Context determines whether the question concerns the speaker's action or what is expected to happen.

correct.text: Shall I turn on the fan?
Should I get a reply by Friday?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Shall and should in direction questions
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An embedded infinitival interrogative presents a question about what to do. A finite counterpart can instead report a request for information.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.6 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Embedded interrogatives do not themselves carry the force of an independent question. Embedded shall does not retain the main-clause direction use.

correct.text: I asked how to unlock the cabinet.
I asked how she unlocked the cabinet.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Rightness of answers to direction questions
statement: A directive answer can settle a choice offered to the addressee or provide advice that can be judged appropriate to the circumstances.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.6 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: An answer that grants or declines an offer need not be assessed in the same way as advice.

correct.text: Shall I hold the door? — Yes, please.
Shall I cycle home in this storm? — Take the bus.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Rightness of answers to direction questions
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Neutral questions and degrees of bias
statement: A biased question presents one answer as favored, whereas a neutral question leaves the options open. Bias can range from a slight inclination to certainty.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.7–4.7.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: If the speaker takes the answer as settled, the question can acknowledge information or convey a statement instead of seeking information.

correct.text: Have you received any notices this month?
The courier has already been here?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Neutral questions and degrees of bias
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A speaker can favor an answer because it seems true, because it ought to be true, or because they want it to be true. These kinds can coexist and favor different answers.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.7.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: In a reproach, the speaker may believe an action was omitted while judging that it ought to have been done.

correct.text: Didn't you lock the cupboard?
May I have some more soup?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Bias can arise from context and prosody or be marked by the grammatical construction. Declarative questions and negative interrogatives are strongly biased in the uses described here.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.7.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Complete bias can also occur in an ordinary interrogative form when the speaker already knows the answer.

correct.text: You haven't heard the news?
Didn't you hear the bell?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A declarative question typically seeks confirmation of the proposition it presents. Its epistemic bias ordinarily follows the polarity of that proposition.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.7.2 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: These forms can also carry a preference or judgment about what should be the case.

correct.text: The gates are open?
The gates aren't open?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Expressions such as surely and of course can reinforce bias without becoming part of the proposition the addressee is asked to confirm.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.7.2 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Confirmatory replies such as Exactly can acknowledge the expected proposition. Comparable items in interrogatives can convey weaker commitment.

correct.text: The plumber has been notified, of course?
You surely kept the receipt?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A declarative used as a question may pragmatically place only its subordinate proposition in question, even when a matrix expression is part of the syntax.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.7.2 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: A matrix qualification can remain outside the inferred question scope. A question about permission can also function as a request.

correct.text: I take it you found the key?
I don't suppose I could borrow your charger?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Negative interrogative form strongly biases a question but does not by itself determine which answer the speaker favors. Context can reverse the epistemic orientation.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.7.3 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: A negative interrogative can indirectly express reproach, apology, or an emphatic exclamatory statement in suitable contexts.

correct.text: Didn't I leave the spare key here?
Isn't that the address you gave me?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: In a positive interrogative, a positively oriented item can make a positive answer more expected or desirable than the corresponding negatively oriented item does.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.7.4 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Already can signal a stronger positive bias than some and its compounds. An offer with some is compatible with a preference for acceptance.

correct.text: Has anyone called about the leak?
Has someone called about the leak?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Negative polarity items in simple positive declarative questions
statement: A simple positive declarative question does not license temporal ever merely by being used as a question.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.7.4 of Chapter 10.
violation: Temporal ever appears in a simple positive declarative question without an independent licensing environment.

exceptions.description: Limit the specification to affirmative declarative syntax with no independent licensor. Preserve interrogative inversion, negative environments, and licensed scalar uses.

correct.text: You've already visited the gallery?
You've already tried the new route?

incorrect.text: You've ever visited the gallery?
You've ever tried the new route?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Negative polarity items in simple positive declarative questions
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

diagnostic.error_pattern: Temporal ever appears in a simple positive declarative question without an independent licensing environment.
minimal_pairs: You've ever visited the gallery? ||| You've already visited the gallery?
You've ever tried the new route? ||| You've already tried the new route?
diagnostic.learner_explanation: A simple positive declarative question does not license temporal ever merely by being used as a question.
diagnostic.corrected_paragraph_template: Keep declarative order with a suitable positive expression, or use interrogative inversion to retain ever.
false_positive_guards: Have you ever visited the gallery?
You haven't ever tried the new route?
It's the best route you've ever tried.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A negatively oriented item can favor the negative answer in a negative interrogative. A positively oriented item can occur with either bias, often with a salient positive interpretation.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.7.4 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The context can still matter for positively oriented forms. Positive orientation also occurs in reminders and indirect exclamations.

correct.text: Haven't they told anyone yet?
Haven't they told someone already?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Echo question types and stimulus modification
statement: A polar echo repeats a stimulus, an alternative echo offers replacements, and a variable echo substitutes a question expression. The echo can shorten the stimulus or adjust pronouns to the new speaker.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.8 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: A changed speaker can require a change in deictic expressions.

correct.text: I repaired the latch. — You repaired the latch?
I left it in the cabinet. — You left it where?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Echo question types and stimulus modification
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Echo questions as indirect speech acts
statement: An echo typically asks about what the previous speaker said or meant. An ordinary question with similar wording can ask about the state of affairs itself.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.8.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Reusing wording from the previous turn is insufficient by itself to establish an echo analysis.

correct.text: Did Lena call? — Did Lena call? I couldn't hear you.
You said the ferry was delayed. Was it delayed?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Echo questions as indirect speech acts
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Form and position of variable echo words
statement: A variable echo word can occupy the position of the echoed expression, even where an ordinary interrogative word cannot occur in that category. It does not trigger inversion by fronting.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.8.2 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Subject echoes and some in-situ ordinary questions can overlap in order. Prosody and context help distinguish them.

correct.text: He was recalibrating it. — He was whatting it?
They left it in the kiln. — They left it in the what?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Form and position of variable echo words
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Variable echo marking can combine with declaratives, interrogatives, exclamatives or imperatives. The echoed construction normally supplies the order and clause-type properties.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.8.2 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: A question word in an echo need not mark an open interrogative clause.

correct.text: Send the receipt to Mina. — Send what to Mina?
Did Omar complain? — Did who complain?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An echo can substitute question expressions for more than one part of its stimulus. Prosody can distinguish several echo words from an ordinary interrogative word plus an echo word.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.8.2 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Ambiguity can remain where the syntactic order is compatible with several analyses.

correct.text: They mailed the maps to Lina. — They mailed what to whom?
Give the bolt to Amir. — Give what to whom?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Polar echoes commonly retain the stimulus form and signal echo meaning through rising intonation. An informal bare predication can reduce the echoed material.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.8.3 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Pronoun subjects in the informal bare-predication pattern tend toward accusative case. Ordinary declarative questions can have the same surface form as a polar echo.

correct.text: The pump failed. — The pump failed?
She's our new mechanic. — Her our new mechanic?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A repetition echo seeks to recover wording that was missed or doubted. A clarification echo asks the speaker to make their intended reference or meaning more explicit.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.8.4 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Clarification can be polar, alternative or variable. Its interpretation and intonation can differ from those of a repetition echo.

correct.text: Put it beside the lathe. — Beside the what?
Put it beside the machine. — Beside which machine?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An interrogative tag or parenthetical is a supplement to an anchor clause and can affect the force of the utterance as a whole.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5–5.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The anchor is commonly declarative, but other clause types occur, including imperatives and exclamatives.

correct.text: The desk is ready, isn't it?
Is the desk ready, do you think?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A reversed polarity tag has polarity opposite to its anchor. A constant polarity tag has the same polarity as its anchor.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Few and hardly can make an anchor negative without overt not. Negative constant polarity tags are not accepted by many speakers.

correct.text: You found the file, didn't you?
So you found the file, did you?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Auxiliary choice and tense in canonical tags
statement: A canonical tag matches the anchor auxiliary and tense, using supportive do where the anchor has a lexical predicator and no auxiliary.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.1 of Chapter 10.
violation: The canonical reversed-polarity tag uses the wrong auxiliary or tense for an unambiguous simple anchor.

exceptions.description: Guard dialectal substitutions, invariant tags, subordinate anchors, imperative tags, and cases where an apparently different tense reflects a different anchor.

correct.text: They can stay, can't they?
She filed it, didn't she?

incorrect.text: They can stay, don't they?
She filed it, doesn't she?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Auxiliary choice and tense in canonical tags
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

diagnostic.error_pattern: The canonical reversed-polarity tag uses the wrong auxiliary or tense for an unambiguous simple anchor.
minimal_pairs: They can stay, don't they? ||| They can stay, can't they?
She filed it, doesn't she? ||| She filed it, didn't she?
diagnostic.learner_explanation: A canonical tag matches the anchor auxiliary and tense, using supportive do where the anchor has a lexical predicator and no auxiliary.
diagnostic.corrected_paragraph_template: Repeat the anchor auxiliary or use do with the anchor tense when the anchor has a lexical verb.
false_positive_guards: I think she filed it, didn't she?
You ought to tell her, shouldn't you?
Close the door, will you?
They can stay, right?

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Agreement with the pronoun in canonical tags
statement: In a canonical tag, the auxiliary agrees with the tag's personal-pronoun subject. That subject is selected in relation to the anchor.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.1 of Chapter 10.
violation: The auxiliary in a canonical tag does not agree with its own subject pronoun.

exceptions.description: Agreement follows the tag pronoun. Singular they and indefinite antecedents may produce different number marking from the anchor.

correct.text: The windows are open, aren't they?
The lamp is on, isn't it?

incorrect.text: The windows are open, isn't they?
The lamp is on, aren't it?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Agreement with the pronoun in canonical tags
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

diagnostic.error_pattern: The auxiliary in a canonical tag does not agree with its own subject pronoun.
minimal_pairs: The windows are open, isn't they? ||| The windows are open, aren't they?
The lamp is on, aren't it? ||| The lamp is on, isn't it?
diagnostic.learner_explanation: In a canonical tag, the auxiliary agrees with the tag's personal-pronoun subject. That subject is selected in relation to the anchor.
diagnostic.corrected_paragraph_template: Choose the auxiliary form that agrees with the tag pronoun.
false_positive_guards: Everybody has arrived, haven't they?
I'm next, aren't I?
The windows are open, right?

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A tag can pick up the subordinate proposition when the matrix expression functions as a qualification of it. Negation in the matrix can affect the interpretation of the subordinate proposition.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Apply the analysis to communicatively foregrounded complements, including some with think, seem or suppose.

correct.text: I think the shutters are closed, aren't they?
I don't think the latch is broken, is it?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Variation in auxiliary choice and anchor form
statement: Some tag forms depart from the canonical auxiliary match. Choices can depend on variety, lexical alternatives and whether the anchor supplies a finite verb.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Most speakers lack mayn't, and there is no single agreed substitute. Have got can take a do tag for some speakers.

correct.text: You ought to tell her, shouldn't you?
Lovely morning, isn't it?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Variation in auxiliary choice and anchor form
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A rising reversed-polarity tag can seek verification, while a falling tag commonly seeks acknowledgment without expressing doubt.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.2 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: A negative anchor with a particular rising contour can express apprehension and favor a positive answer. Punctuation alone does not distinguish the contours.

correct.text: The meter is still running, isn't it? — I can't tell from here.
It's cold in here, isn't it? — It certainly is.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Constant polarity tags and prior discourse
statement: A constant polarity tag can signal surprise, acknowledgment or reproach when the anchor proposition comes from earlier discourse or is attributed to the addressee.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.2 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Reproach is optional. Exclamative anchors normally favor reversed-polarity tags.

correct.text: So you've ordered a second desk, have you?
The spare parts have arrived, have they?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Constant polarity tags and prior discourse
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A parenthetical can follow or interrupt an independent anchor. A corresponding integrated construction instead uses that material as a subordinate complement.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.3 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Parentheticals lack the complement of their integrated counterparts and normally background the qualification.

correct.text: I think the bridge is safe.
The bridge is, I think, safe.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An interrogative parenthetical can request confirmation of a declarative anchor or qualify the interpretation of an interrogative anchor. The latter usually conveys one question overall.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.3 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The corresponding integrated question can instead be about what somebody said. In the surveyed pattern, do you know as a parenthetical takes a closed interrogative anchor.

correct.text: The route is clear, don't you think?
When will the train arrive, did she say?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An interrogative parenthetical can identify an echo as seeking repetition or clarification without adding a second independent question.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.3 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The integrated form can have a different clause structure and communicative interpretation.

correct.text: She ordered what, did you say?
Use the blue folder, do you mean?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An information question ordinarily presupposes a right answer. An alternative question presents a set of mutually exclusive candidate answers and ordinarily presupposes that one applies.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6–6.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: An explicit both option adds an alternative and makes the earlier options exclusive of the combined choice.

correct.text: Will you drive or take the train?
Would you like crackers, grapes, or both?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A polar question's question–answer presupposition is the disjunction of a proposition and its negation. This is logically exhaustive, but asking can still pragmatically signal that one possibility cannot be taken for granted.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.2 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The same disjunction underlies the positive and negative formulations. An indirect accusation can arise pragmatically.

correct.text: Did the package arrive?
Didn't the package arrive?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A variable question normally presupposes a suitable value exists. Replacing its variable with a matching indefinite can represent that presupposition.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.3 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The domain of the indefinite follows the interrogative word. The indefinite proposition does not itself supply a particular answer.

correct.text: Who signed the receipt?
When did the courier leave?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A response supports the presupposition of a variable question when it supplies a value in the relevant domain. A true proposition can fail to answer when it lacks that property.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.3 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: For an elliptical reply, the listener may need to infer an additional domain-membership premise.

correct.text: Which plumber repaired the tap? — Rosa repaired it.
Which plumber repaired the tap? — Rosa repaired it, but she's an electrician.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A response can reject the presupposition of a question by denying that any listed alternative or suitable value applies.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.4 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: A negative quantificational reply can reject the existence of a value without furnishing one.

correct.text: Will you walk or cycle? — Neither. I'm staying here.
Who delivered the parcel? — Nobody. It's still at the depot.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A variable question can be used without its ordinary existence presupposition. This is possible in rhetorical challenges and some conventional indirect statements.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.5 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Should can occur with or without cancellation. Interpretation depends on context.

correct.text: Why should she sign that?
How should I know?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Negatively oriented items and some bare infinitival why questions can signal that the speaker takes no suitable value for granted.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.5 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: A finite negative why question can preserve the presupposition, for example when it seeks the reason for a present preference.

correct.text: Where could we find anything quieter?
Why postpone the launch?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A question can carry background assumptions from its predicate or another construction in addition to its ordinary question–answer presupposition.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.6 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The first ordinarily assumes prior cycling, and the second ordinarily assumes that the deletion happened. These assumptions depend on the wording.

correct.text: Has Mira stopped cycling to work?
Did Max erase the file deliberately?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Interrogative role and core syntactic role
statement: An interrogative word marks a question variable and also plays a role within the clause, such as heading an NP or determining a nominal.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Interrogative subordinators belong to a different class. Who and whom are case forms of one lexeme in this analysis.

correct.text: Who borrowed the spanner?
What tools did you borrow?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Interrogative role and core syntactic role
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Selection from a definite set with which
statement: Which asks for a value selected from a definite set recoverable from the wording or context.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The set need not be stated explicitly in the question. The next page develops explicit set expressions.

correct.text: Which drawer contains the tape?
Which do you prefer?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Selection from a definite set with which
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Interrogative which can take a partitive whose complement identifies the set by a definite NP or an enumeration of its members. A cardinal can specify how many members to select.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.1 of Chapter 10.
violation: A which partitive takes an indefinite NP in place of an identifiable set expression.

exceptions.description: Out of can replace of in some examples. Do not confuse the set-denoting complement with an indefinite NP elsewhere in the clause.

correct.text: Which two of these switches are faulty?
Which of these woods would you use?

incorrect.text: Which two of some switches are faulty?
Which of some woods would you use?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

diagnostic.error_pattern: A which partitive takes an indefinite NP in place of an identifiable set expression.
minimal_pairs: Which two of some switches are faulty? ||| Which two of these switches are faulty?
Which of some woods would you use? ||| Which of these woods would you use?
diagnostic.learner_explanation: Interrogative which can take a partitive whose complement identifies the set by a definite NP or an enumeration of its members. A cardinal can specify how many members to select.
diagnostic.corrected_paragraph_template: Use a definite set expression or enumerate the members in the partitive.
false_positive_guards: Which of cedar, pine, and oak would you use?
Which of them did you try?
Which out of the spare parts fits?
Which switches are faulty?

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Contextual sets with which and what
statement: Which encodes selection from an identifiable set, even when the set is supplied by the context. What can sometimes ask the same practical question without encoding the set restriction.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The contrast is clearer when which has an explicit partitive. A familiar, limited set can make the difference pragmatically small.

correct.text: Which route did you take?
What route did you take?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Contextual sets with which and what
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Interrogative whose is a personal genitive. It can determine a following noun, serve predicatively, or fuse determiner and head when the noun is recoverable.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.2 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Fused use is relatively infrequent, and the explicit partitive available with which is generally unavailable with whose.

correct.text: Whose umbrella is on the rack?
Whose is the striped one?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Who and whom and the contrast with which
statement: Who and whom are personal interrogative heads. Which can select an individual from an identified group, while who can ask for the person's identity.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.3 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The intended readings can overlap. Who permits some full partitives with of or out of, so a general ban on partitives with who would be too strong.

correct.text: Who is the new supervisor?
Which is the new supervisor?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Who and whom and the contrast with which
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: In a specifying question about a person, who asks for an identity. What in an ascriptive question can ask about a relevant category, such as occupation.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.3 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The relevant category of properties depends on the discourse.

correct.text: Who is Rina? — She's the project lead.
What is Rina? — She's an architect.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: When questions time as an adjunct, a complement, or an element of a specifying construction. It can also complement a preposition.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.4 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Since when may challenge a claimed situation rather than merely seek its starting date.

correct.text: When will the shop reopen?
Since when have you had the key?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Where can question location or goal and has a range of clause functions comparable to temporal when. It can be the complement of a spatial preposition.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.5 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Fronted from where is markedly formal in the illustrated contrast. At is available in some uses and varieties.

correct.text: Where should we put the ladder?
Where did you come from?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Why questions reason or purpose as an adjunct or in a reason cleft. A specifying question asking for the identity of a reason instead uses what.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.6 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Informal what for can replace adjunct why, subject to the construction. It does not directly substitute for why in the reason cleft.

correct.text: Why did you close the shutters?
What was the reason for the delay?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Why can introduce a suggestion or challenge without presupposing an available reason. As a response to a directive or question, it can ask why the prior act was performed or why one should comply.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.6 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Why is restricted in the direction and infinitival patterns discussed here. A reason for asking can be requested separately from the information sought by the original question.

correct.text: Why not wait until morning?
Check the back door. — Why?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Predicative and degree uses of how
statement: Adjectival how can ask about a subject or object predicative complement. Adverbial how can modify gradable expressions and ask for a point on a scale.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.7 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Degree how modifies relatively few verbs directly. How much is available more broadly, and different scale adjectives carry different presuppositions.

correct.text: How was the rehearsal?
How tightly did you fasten the clamp?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Predicative and degree uses of how
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: How can question the means by which an event is accomplished or the manner in which it unfolds. A predicative use instead asks for a characterization.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.7 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The verb and context can support more than one reading.

correct.text: How did you open it? — With a spare key.
How did she speak? — Quietly.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: How can request evidence with verbs such as know and expressions such as be sure. In a reason cleft it can overlap with why.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.7 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: An evidence question can challenge a claim without presupposing that the addressee has adequate evidence.

correct.text: How do you know the hinge is loose?
How is it that the gate always sticks?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Clause order after idiomatic how come
statement: Informal how come introduces a reason question with ordinary subject–predicator order.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.7 of Chapter 10.
violation: The subject and auxiliary are inverted after idiomatic how come.

exceptions.description: Distinguish idiomatic how come from a standard inverted why question and from a compositional construction with the verb come.

correct.text: How come the gate is locked?
How come Maya left early?

incorrect.text: How come is the gate locked?
How come did Maya leave early?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Clause order after idiomatic how come
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

diagnostic.error_pattern: The subject and auxiliary are inverted after idiomatic how come.
minimal_pairs: How come is the gate locked? ||| How come the gate is locked?
How come did Maya leave early? ||| How come Maya left early?
diagnostic.learner_explanation: Informal how come introduces a reason question with ordinary subject–predicator order.
diagnostic.corrected_paragraph_template: Use ordinary clause order after how come, adjusting the lexical verb if do-support was added.
false_positive_guards: Why is the gate locked?
How did it come to be locked?
How come Maya did leave early after all?

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: How about and other how idioms
statement: How about can introduce a suggestion or bring another participant or topic into a discussion. Other formulas with how can have conventional force beyond an ordinary information question.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.7 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The construction is informal and can take an NP, a gerund-participial expression, or a finite clause.

correct.text: How about taking a break?
I prefer the early train. How about you?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: How about and other how idioms
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Interrogative what can determine a following noun or serve as a pronoun heading an NP. Its lexical contrasts depend on the role.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.8 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Interrogative what differs from which in selectivity and from who in its ordinary nonpersonal use.

correct.text: What paint did you use?
What did you find?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Verbless what and what if constructions
statement: What can stand alone as a reduced question, an echo, or an acknowledgment. What about can raise a topic, and what if can raise a possible situation for consideration.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.8 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Context distinguishes echo from ordinary reduction. So what conventionally challenges relevance.

correct.text: I found something. — What?
What if the shop closes before we arrive?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Verbless what and what if constructions
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: The interrogative feature can extend from a word through nested phrases. When fronting applies, the maximal interrogative phrase moves together.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.9 of Chapter 10.
violation: A smaller interrogative phrase fronts while the remainder of its maximal nominal phrase is left behind.

exceptions.description: This account allows more than one level of interrogative phrase within a single constituent.

correct.text: What size boots did you order?
How large a crate did they build?

incorrect.text: What size did you order boots?
How large did they build a crate?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

diagnostic.error_pattern: A smaller interrogative phrase fronts while the remainder of its maximal nominal phrase is left behind.
minimal_pairs: What size did you order boots? ||| What size boots did you order?
How large did they build a crate? ||| How large a crate did they build?
diagnostic.learner_explanation: The interrogative feature can extend from a word through nested phrases. When fronting applies, the maximal interrogative phrase moves together.
diagnostic.corrected_paragraph_template: Front the complete nominal interrogative phrase in the intended question.
false_positive_guards: What size did you order?
You ordered what size boots?
How large did they build it?

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Stranded and fronted prepositions in interrogatives
statement: An interrogative NP can front with the preposition stranded, or a containing PP can front in a more formal construction.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.9 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Nested structures can allow fronting of a higher PP. The corresponding bare NP containing an embedded interrogative PP is not generally a frontable alternative.

correct.text: Which shelf did you put it on?
On which shelf did you put it?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Stranded and fronted prepositions in interrogatives
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: The grammatical unit fronted in a question can be larger than the expression replaced to form an answer.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.10 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: A PP often retains its preposition in the answer. Idioms such as what for and what like can instead be answered by replacing the whole PP.

correct.text: Whose laptop is charging? — Farah's laptop is charging.
With whom did you travel? — I traveled with Farah.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Questions built with do or happen can seek a predication rather than an NP replacement for what. A following PP can identify the participant involved.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.10 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Do with can ask how something was disposed of or placed. Happen to allows a wider range of participant roles than an affected patient alone.

correct.text: What did you do to the latch? — I tightened its screws.
What happened to the parcel? — It fell off the cart.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A fronted interrogative phrase can be linked to a gap within an embedded clause, including across more than one clause boundary.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.11–7.12 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The number of intervening clauses is not fixed in principle. This does not eliminate independent restrictions on where gaps can occur.

correct.text: What did Arun buy?
What do you think Arun said he wanted to buy?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: The same fronted interrogative phrase can have different core roles, including attachment to a higher or lower clause.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.12 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Adjunct attachment is a common source of ambiguity. Some complements also permit distinct roles in restricted configurations.

correct.text: When did they decide to depart?
Why do you think the pump stopped?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Scope of in-situ phrases in multi-variable questions
statement: In a complex multi-variable question, an in-situ interrogative phrase can be interpreted with a higher question or with an embedded question.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.12 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: An answer can pair informants with values or identify someone who knows all relevant pairings, depending on scope.

correct.text: Who knows which shops stock which parts?
Who can tell me which trains stop at which stations?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Scope of in-situ phrases in multi-variable questions
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A limited set of modifiers can follow interrogative words to emphasize uncertainty, add alternatives, or request precision.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.13 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The available modifier depends on the interrogative word and placement. Else can occur in constructions unavailable to some emphatic modifiers.

correct.text: Who on earth left the tap running?
What exactly did you order?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Subject and predicative complement in be questions
statement: A clause beginning with an interrogative NP and be can have an interrogative subject or a fronted predicative complement. Modal insertion or embedding can help distinguish the structures.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.14 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Some specifying and ascriptive cases remain structurally ambiguous. Pronoun case can provide a clue in suitable examples.

correct.text: Who will be treasurer?
What time will it be?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Subject and predicative complement in be questions
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Exclamative phrases and obligatory non-subject fronting
statement: What and how mark exclamative phrases. An exclamative subject stays in subject position, while a non-subject exclamative phrase occurs initially and can link to an embedded gap.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §8.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Preposition stranding and fronting both occur in the appropriate exclamative patterns. Certain subject exclamatives resemble interrogatives in writing.

correct.text: What unusual birds live here!
How expensive she expected the repairs to be!

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Exclamative phrases and obligatory non-subject fronting
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Exclamative how presents degree as remarkable and can modify an adjective, adverb, degree determinative, or degree modifier.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §8.1.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: An interrogative degree question instead asks for a value on the scale. The exclamative pattern permits a degree modifier after how.

correct.text: How quickly the pond froze!
How very carefully she packed the glass!

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: When how modifies the verb in an exclamative, it expresses remarkable degree. In a corresponding ordinary interrogative, how can question means or manner.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §8.1.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Inversion with verb-modifying how in the illustrated contrast gives the interrogative analysis.

correct.text: How they admired her!
How did they persuade her?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Exclamative what and singular count NPs
statement: Exclamative what modifies an NP. With a singular count noun in the illustrated pattern, what precedes a or an. Plural and non-count patterns lack that article.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §8.1.2 of Chapter 10.
violation: A singular count NP modified by exclamative what is missing a or an.

exceptions.description: Guard interrogative what, plural and non-count exclamatives, fused relatives, and fixed formulas outside this pattern.

correct.text: What a strange noise it made!
What an unusual instrument she found!

incorrect.text: What strange noise it made!
What unusual instrument she found!

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Exclamative what and singular count NPs
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

diagnostic.error_pattern: A singular count NP modified by exclamative what is missing a or an.
minimal_pairs: What strange noise it made! ||| What a strange noise it made!
What unusual instrument she found! ||| What an unusual instrument she found!
diagnostic.learner_explanation: Exclamative what modifies an NP. With a singular count noun in the illustrated pattern, what precedes a or an. Plural and non-count patterns lack that article.
diagnostic.corrected_paragraph_template: Place a or an after exclamative what in this singular count pattern.
false_positive_guards: What strange noises it made!
What beautiful music she found!
What instrument did she find?
What she found!

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Quality and distribution of exclamative what
statement: Exclamative what presents quality or degree as remarkable. It modifies an NP directly, whereas a how phrase can be an external modifier of a singular count NP.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §8.1.2 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Approval or disapproval is inferred from context. Exclamative how tends toward more formal style.

correct.text: What beautiful handwriting she has!
How elegant a solution it was!

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Quality and distribution of exclamative what
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Subject position and inversion in exclamatives
statement: A fronted non-subject exclamative phrase usually precedes ordinary subject–predicator order. Some literary exclamatives permit inversion or, in a distinct pattern, a postposed subject.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §8.1.3 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: An inverted sequence with an exclamation mark can instead be a rhetorical interrogative. Punctuation alone cannot settle the analysis.

correct.text: What a racket the fan made!
What a surprise would it have been if the doors had opened!

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Subject position and inversion in exclamatives
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An exclamative can consist of the exclamative phrase alone or include an additional clause interpreted in relation to an understood predication.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §8.1.4 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: A following infinitival can be relative in one pattern and an extraposed subject in another. The source also records less common gerund-participial cases.

correct.text: What an odd coincidence!
How strange that nobody called!

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An exclamative normally foregrounds the speaker's evaluation or reaction while presenting the underlying situation as given. It is conventionally an exclamatory statement.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §8.2 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: A falling tag can invite agreement with the evaluation. Echoes aside, an answer does not normally supply a value for the exclamative expression.

correct.text: How bright the room is now!
What a mess they've made!
