review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Closed interrogatives and clauses with so or such can convey exclamatory force through their wording and prosody. Their ordinary syntax can remain intact.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §8.3 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: So and such do not obligatorily front and can occur outside declaratives in appropriate constructions.

correct.text: Wasn't that an extraordinary finish!
They were so patient!

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Some NPs or fused relatives stand as exclamations and can correspond to extraposed NPs. An imprecative retort can use an expletive followed by a pronoun and auxiliary with an understood complement.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §8.3 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The NP type often conveys disapproval. The retort is strongly informal.

correct.text: The prices they charge for repairs!
I'll cancel the booking. — Like hell you will!

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Imperatives allow an optional subject, a plain verb form, and supportive do even with be in the relevant constructions. Let marks a subtype with properties explored separately.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Lexical let meaning allow remains available in ordinary imperatives. The apparent similarity of the forms does not settle the analysis.

correct.text: Keep the corridor clear.
Let's keep the corridor clear.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Inclusive let-imperatives normally include speaker and addressee. Open let-imperatives can express a directive about a third party or another participant without specifically addressing that participant.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.1–9.2.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: An ordinary imperative with lexical let can ask the addressee to permit an action.

correct.text: Let's open the windows.
Let the winning team speak first.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An ordinary imperative can omit its subject, usually understood as the addressee. It can also contain second- or third-person subjects.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.2.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The plain verb form distinguishes many third-person singular imperatives from declaratives. Some other cases are formally ambiguous.

correct.text: Lock the gate before you leave.
Everybody check the back of your ticket.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Restrictions and discourse functions of overt subjects
statement: Overt imperative subjects commonly denote people, and indefinite expressions such as everybody and nobody are frequent. An explicit you can identify a participant or reinforce reassurance or insistence.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.2.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The distribution of definite third-person subjects depends on context. Dummy and clausal subjects are excluded from the illustrated ordinary imperative construction.

correct.text: Nobody touch the switch.
You take the first watch, and I'll take the second.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Restrictions and discourse functions of overt subjects
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An optional subject is integrated into the clause, while a vocative directly addresses a participant and can be prosodically separate. Both can occur in one imperative.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.2.2 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: With some initial NPs either analysis is possible. Final integrated NPs and anaphora can provide mixed evidence, so punctuation is not conclusive.

correct.text: Nobody move, please.
Maya, you take the front seat.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Scope and placement in negative imperatives
statement: Imperative negation generally uses do not or don't. With an overt subject, the subject can precede don't or follow it, with possible differences in scope and interpretation.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.2.3 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: With uncontracted do not, a subject between do and not gives the interrogative order. Uncontracted do not followed by overt you is also marked.

correct.text: Those without a ticket don't enter yet.
Don't anybody touch the switch.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Scope and placement in negative imperatives
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Positive imperative do emphasizes the directive and can occur with be as well as lexical verbs.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.2.3 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: With some overt subjects, emphatic do may follow or precede the subject. Prosody and context influence how the emphasis is understood.

correct.text: Do be careful on the steps.
Do call before you leave.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An imperative directive presents a possible action for compliance. Orders and commands demand compliance, while requests conventionally present it as optional.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.2.4 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Institutional authority and context distinguish a command from other strong directives. A negative order can function as a prohibition.

correct.text: Report to the front desk at once.
Please lend me a pencil.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Advice presents an action as serving the addressee's interests. Instructions specify steps for a goal, and expository imperatives guide the audience through a discussion.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.2.4 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Advice can include warnings. Expository directives seek participation in following the exposition.

correct.text: Keep a spare key somewhere safe.
Compare the two diagrams before reading on.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An imperative can invite an action, grant permission for it, or signal acceptance of a choice the addressee has proposed.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.2.4 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: These uses can give the addressee a choice. Their force depends on prior discourse and the speaker's stance.

correct.text: Have another slice if you'd like.
Go ahead and borrow the ladder.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Directive imperatives usually concern future action under the addressee's control, so dynamic VPs are typical. The construction can also encourage an agentive reading of a normally stative predicate.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.2.5 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Progressive and perfect imperatives are relatively infrequent, but rarity is not a categorical ban. Causative have differs from perfect have.

correct.text: Finish the draft by Monday.
Be patient while the glue dries.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A passive imperative can direct the addressee to take or avoid action that brings about a passive outcome.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.2.5 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Negative be passives and get passives can support agentive readings. A construction with a reflexive object is syntactically distinct.

correct.text: Don't be seen near the side door.
Get examined by a qualified technician.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An imperative with little or no plausible control by the addressee can conventionally express a wish or another indirect force.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.2.5 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The same wording can be a directive in an appropriate context, and a directive can accompany a wish.

correct.text: Sleep well.
Have a wonderful holiday!

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: One variety analyzes inclusive let with us, optionally contracted to 's, and a bare infinitival complement. Another also permits a following overt NP with reanalyzed let's.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.3.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The second example belongs to the variety allowing the overt NP. The more conservative variety lacks that pattern.

correct.text: Let's repair the fence ourselves.
Let's you and me repair the fence ourselves.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Subject and ellipsis properties of conservative inclusive let
statement: In the conservative inclusive construction, an overt matrix subject is unavailable, and the let element is retained when the following predication is ellipted.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.3.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: An ordinary lexical let imperative can have a matrix subject. Conservative inclusive ellipsis differs from ordinary imperative echo responses.

correct.text: Let's take the shortcut, shall we?
Let's take the shortcut. — No, let's not.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Subject and ellipsis properties of conservative inclusive let
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Negation in inclusive and lexical let constructions
statement: With inclusive let's, the two illustrated placements of negation can convey the same proposal. With lexical let, negation placement can distinguish withholding permission from permitting a negative action.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.3.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Don't let's is stylistically more informal and varies across speakers. Lexical Don't let them leave and Let them not leave can differ in scope.

correct.text: Let's not wait here.
Don't let's wait here.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Negation in inclusive and lexical let constructions
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An inclusive imperative normally proposes action involving both speaker and addressee and invites their agreement. In exposition it can present a step as shared.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.3.2 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: An immediate verbal response is typical for an ordinary proposal but not required in an expository use.

correct.text: Let's move the table together.
Let's now compare the two totals.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Open let and its boundary with lexical let
statement: Open let can present a directive without assigning responsibility specifically to the addressee. It also occurs in formulaic, expository and other uses.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.4 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The boundary with lexical allow is gradual, and the chapter considers a meaning-based alternative analysis.

correct.text: Let the records show that we objected.
Let x be the length of the shorter side.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Open let and its boundary with lexical let
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Imperative first coordinates with conditional interpretations
statement: An imperative can be the first coordinate in a construction whose overall force is conditional. With and, the next coordinate can give a consequence of compliance.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.5 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The first imperative need not independently direct the action. An interpretation as warning or threat can depend on context.

correct.text: Press that switch and the screen will go dark.
Take another step and you'll set off the alarm.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Imperative first coordinates with conditional interpretations
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: In conditional coordination, an imperative can have a subject or predicate disfavored in a standalone directive, and the consequence can use several clause types.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.5 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The imperative can be negative in some contexts. Let-imperatives vary in their compatibility with this conditional use.

correct.text: Leave the windows open and what a mess there'll be!
Follow that path and who will find you?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Ability and willingness questions as directives
statement: Interrogatives about ability, desire or willingness can indirectly request an action. Tentative modal preterites can make a request more polite.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.6.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The literal question can remain salient when the ability or willingness is genuinely uncertain. Negative forms can sound impatient or reproachful.

correct.text: Could you pass me the folder?
Would you mind lowering the blinds?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Ability and willingness questions as directives
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Necessity and reason questions as directives
statement: A question about whether an unwanted action is necessary, or whether it has a reason, can indirectly discourage that action.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.6.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Negative reason questions can instead propose the positive action. Directive interrogatives also allow some third-person subjects.

correct.text: Do you have to play the music so loudly?
Why leave the door wide open?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Necessity and reason questions as directives
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A first-person plural interrogative can propose joint action in much the same pragmatic role as an inclusive let-imperative.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.6.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The interrogative construction can retain its ordinary question use in a suitable context.

correct.text: Shall we try the shorter route?
Why don't we take a break?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Declaratives as direct and indirect directives
statement: A declarative can perform a directive through an overt performative or prohibition. It can also convey one indirectly by stating a want, necessity or tentative inquiry.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.6.2 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: A declarative can embed a question that itself conveys the directive indirectly. The surrounding context helps establish force.

correct.text: I forbid you to enter the storage room.
I wonder whether you would close the window.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Declaratives as direct and indirect directives
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Notices and brief requests can express directives using nonfinite clauses or verbless expressions.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.6.3 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: An abbreviated passive notice can correspond to a finite prohibition. A verbless expression can also occur in spoken orders.

correct.text: Visitors prohibited beyond this gate.
Two tickets, please.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Ordinary imperatives can take tags with forms such as will you, would you or can you. Choice affects tone, and tag polarity does not follow declarative reversal rules mechanically.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.7 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Positive anchors allow either tag polarity in the relevant uses. Negative ordinary imperative anchors normally take positive will you.

correct.text: Hand me the receipt, would you?
Don't touch the dial, will you?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An inclusive let-imperative typically takes shall we. An alternative tag in the illustrated construction is why don't we.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.7 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The inclusive pattern differs from the second-person tags used with ordinary imperatives.

correct.text: Let's check the figures, shall we?
Let's take the stairs, why don't we?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Reporting directives without a subordinate imperative
statement: Directives can be reported through infinitivals or mandative content clauses, but these are distinct constructions with broader distributions than main imperatives.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.8 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The matrix predicate contributes the directive interpretation. Mandatives can have subjects and predicate patterns that ordinary imperatives do not license.

correct.text: She told us to close the gate.
She insisted that we be ready at eight.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Reporting directives without a subordinate imperative
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Minor optative patterns can express wishes with initial may or with formulaic plain-form constructions.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §10 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Some optatives are highly formulaic. A wish can also be expressed with an imperative in other constructions.

correct.text: May your journey be peaceful.
Long live the festival!

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Some minor main clauses have forms otherwise associated with subordination, including that clauses and restricted to-infinitival formulas.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §10 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The constructional range is limited. The negative infinitival formula is largely restricted to worry.

correct.text: That it should end like this!
Not to worry.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A conditional adjunct can stand without an expressed consequence and convey regret, surprise, a request, or a hypothetical prompt.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §10 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The intended force depends on the conditional form and context. A fragment is not necessarily an unfinished sentence in discourse.

correct.text: If only you'd called sooner!
If you'd like to step this way.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Verbless directives and parallel minor structures
statement: Some independent expressions function as directives without a verb. Parallel expressions can also express a conditional relation or another connection without a full ordinary clause structure.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §10 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Some verbless directives correspond to ordinary imperatives with an understood verb. Parallel forms also occur in fixed sayings.

correct.text: Off the stage!
No key, no entry.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Verbless directives and parallel minor structures
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: No overt matrix subject before inclusive let's
statement: The inclusive let's construction does not take an overt matrix subject before let's.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.3.1 of Chapter 10.
violation: An integrated matrix subject precedes inclusive let’s.

exceptions.description: A detached vocative can precede let's. Some varieties allow an overt subject after reanalyzed let's, and ordinary lexical let has different subject possibilities.

correct.text: Let's review the figures.
Let's wait for the others.

incorrect.text: You let's review the figures.
We let's wait for the others.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: No overt matrix subject before inclusive let's
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

diagnostic.error_pattern: An integrated matrix subject precedes inclusive let’s.
minimal_pairs: You let's review the figures. ||| Let's review the figures.
We let's wait for the others. ||| Let's wait for the others.
diagnostic.learner_explanation: The inclusive let's construction does not take an overt matrix subject before let's.
diagnostic.corrected_paragraph_template: Remove the integrated subject in the inclusive construction.
false_positive_guards: Maya, let's review the figures.
You let her review the figures.
Let's you and me wait outside.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Conditional consequences with and and or
statement: In the illustrated coordination, and can introduce a consequence of doing what the imperative describes. Or can introduce a consequence of failing to comply while the imperative retains its directive force.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.5 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Conditional meaning comes from the coordination and context. It is not a fixed meaning of imperative clause type.

correct.text: Check the register and you'll see her name.
Leave now or you'll miss the bus.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Conditional consequences with and and or
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Negating a to-infinitival report of a directive
statement: In an ordinary to-infinitival report of a negative directive, use not without importing the imperative's supportive do.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9.8 of Chapter 10.
violation: Imperative supportive do is retained within an ordinary negative to-infinitival report.

exceptions.description: An independent quoted imperative can retain don't. Finite subordinate clauses and lexical do have different distributions.

correct.text: Mina told me not to be late.
Omar asked us not to touch the dial.

incorrect.text: Mina told me to do not be late.
Omar asked us to do not touch the dial.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Negating a to-infinitival report of a directive
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

diagnostic.error_pattern: Imperative supportive do is retained within an ordinary negative to-infinitival report.
minimal_pairs: Mina told me to do not be late. ||| Mina told me not to be late.
Omar asked us to do not touch the dial. ||| Omar asked us not to touch the dial.
diagnostic.learner_explanation: In an ordinary to-infinitival report of a negative directive, use not without importing the imperative's supportive do.
diagnostic.corrected_paragraph_template: Use not to followed by the plain form of the lexical verb.
false_positive_guards: Mina said, ‘Don't be late.’
I asked why they didn't touch the dial.
She told me not to do the paperwork.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A plain verb form can head a finite imperative or subjunctive as well as a non-finite infinitival. Clause structure is needed to distinguish them.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: A clause headed by a present tense, preterite or irrealis were is finite. Gerund-participial and past-participial heads give non-finite clauses.

correct.text: Be ready at noon.
We asked them to be ready at noon.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Infinitival, gerund-participial and past-participial clauses are distinguished by their head forms. Infinitivals are further divided according to whether they contain to.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Bare infinitivals have restricted distribution, including complements of modal auxiliaries and supportive do.

correct.text: I remember locking the gate.
They had the lock replaced.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Auxiliary and voice options in non-finites
statement: Infinitivals permit perfect, progressive and passive auxiliaries. Gerund-participials permit perfect and passive auxiliaries, while progressive being is marginal.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Past-participial clauses headed by perfect been and those headed by a passive participle have different auxiliary possibilities. Modal auxiliaries and supportive do are excluded from non-finite clauses themselves.

correct.text: They seem to have been waiting.
She recalled being warned.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Auxiliary and voice options in non-finites
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A VP can constitute a clause without an overt subject. A restricted attributive VP inside an NP is analyzed separately as a VP without clause status.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Prenominal attributive VPs have much more limited expansion than clause modifiers.

correct.text: Anyone waiting outside may come in.
The rapidly approaching storm delayed the ferry.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Hollow clauses and other infinitival structures
statement: A hollow non-finite clause lacks a non-subject element interpreted from elsewhere. Infinitival form also occurs in subordinate interrogatives and relative clauses.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Hollow status depends on the missing non-subject element. The absence of an overt subject alone does not establish it.

correct.text: The shelf was too high for me to reach.
I asked which shelf to use.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Hollow clauses and other infinitival structures
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Non-finite clauses can be complements in several phrase types or function as modifiers and supplements.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1.1–1.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: A purpose clause with in order to and a bare purpose adjunct can have similar meanings and different internal structures.

correct.text: She was eager to return.
She left early to catch the train.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A catenative verb licenses a non-finite internal complement. Repetition of this relation allows chains with several verbs.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: A verb at the end of the chain need not itself license a non-finite complement. The chapter treats the catenative complement as a distinct function.

correct.text: We hoped to try to repair it.
She began to explain the delay.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Auxiliaries and simple versus complex catenatives
statement: Auxiliary uses fit the catenative analysis. An active catenative construction is simple or complex according to the absence or presence of an intervening NP.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: A passive corresponding to a complex active remains in the complex class even without an NP between the verbs.

correct.text: I expected to win.
I expected her to win.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Auxiliaries and simple versus complex catenatives
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: The complex construction includes for, oblique, genitive and plain subtypes. The intervening NP can belong to the matrix or subordinate clause according to the construction.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: An oblique NP is the complement of a selected preposition. Plain or accusative NPs can have different functions in different constructions.

correct.text: We arranged for them to depart.
I resented their leaving early.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: For and overt subjects in to-infinitivals
statement: In the standard construction, an overt subject internal to a to-infinitival is introduced by for. An infinitival without such a subject does not take this for.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1.3 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: A preceding matrix object does not count as an infinitival subject. Some nonstandard varieties have for to without an intervening subject.

correct.text: For Mina to leave now would be awkward.
To leave now would be awkward.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: For and overt subjects in to-infinitivals
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: The NP in a plain-complex to-infinitival construction is a matrix object, while the NP after infinitival for is the subordinate subject.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1.3 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Expect excludes for, arrange selects it in the overt-subject pattern, and intend permits both structures.

correct.text: We expected the ferry to depart at six.
We arranged for the ferry to depart at six.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Passivization as a test for the intervening NP
statement: A matrix object can be eligible for promotion in a corresponding passive. The whole for-clause can instead behave as a constituent in appropriate extraposition patterns.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1.3 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Passive promotion is not a necessary property of every object. Want has independent restrictions on passive formation.

correct.text: The ferry was expected to depart at six.
It was arranged for the ferry to depart at six.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Passivization as a test for the intervening NP
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Adjunct and omission tests for complex structures
statement: Matrix adjunct placement, pseudo-clefting and omission provide evidence for distinguishing a matrix object from a subordinate subject.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1.3 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Some plain-complex verbs require the object even with coreference. With persuade the NP also has a semantic role in the matrix clause.

correct.text: They arranged at once for Jo to speak.
They persuaded Jo to speak.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Adjunct and omission tests for complex structures
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Infinitival for introduces a clause nucleus containing a subject and predicate. Distribution and the possibility of dummy there distinguish it from prepositional for.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1.4.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: For PPs and for-infinitivals share some environments. Some strings admit either attachment, depending on interpretation.

correct.text: For there to be a delay would be unusual.
We asked for the inspection to be postponed.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A personal pronoun used as the subject of a for-infinitival takes accusative case when the pronoun distinguishes case.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1.4.1 of Chapter 14.
violation: A nominative personal pronoun appears as the subject of a for-infinitival.

exceptions.description: Scope is limited to simple personal-pronoun subjects in this construction. Dummy there and ordinary noun phrases do not show this case contrast.

correct.text: We arranged for him to speak first.
It was unusual for her to arrive late.

incorrect.text: We arranged for he to speak first.
It was unusual for she to arrive late.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

diagnostic.error_pattern: A nominative personal pronoun appears as the subject of a for-infinitival.
minimal_pairs: We arranged for he to speak first. ||| We arranged for him to speak first.
It was unusual for she to arrive late. ||| It was unusual for her to arrive late.
diagnostic.learner_explanation: A personal pronoun used as the subject of a for-infinitival takes accusative case when the pronoun distinguishes case.
diagnostic.corrected_paragraph_template: Use the accusative form of the pronoun after infinitival for.
false_positive_guards: We arranged for there to be a break.
We arranged for both speakers to attend.
We arranged that he would speak first.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Position of for and its infinitival subject
statement: Infinitival for occupies initial position in its clause, and the subject NP immediately follows it.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1.4.1 of Chapter 14.
violation: An object of the infinitival verb occurs between clause-marker for and the subject NP.

exceptions.description: Unlike finite that clauses, these clauses do not allow a clause element to front across the subject.

correct.text: It is essential for you to check the pressure first.
It is essential for them to test the seal next.

incorrect.text: It is essential for the pressure you to check first.
It is essential for the seal them to test next.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Position of for and its infinitival subject
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

diagnostic.error_pattern: An object of the infinitival verb occurs between clause-marker for and the subject NP.
minimal_pairs: It is essential for the pressure you to check first. ||| It is essential for you to check the pressure first.
It is essential for the seal them to test next. ||| It is essential for them to test the seal next.
diagnostic.learner_explanation: Infinitival for occupies initial position in its clause, and the subject NP immediately follows it.
diagnostic.corrected_paragraph_template: Put the subject immediately after for and keep the object after the infinitival verb.
false_positive_guards: It is essential that the pressure you check first.
It is essential for both of you to check the pressure.
It is essential for you to first check the pressure.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Infinitival to combines with a VP
statement: Fronting, ellipsis and coordination support treating to as combining with a VP rather than forming a morphological unit with the following verb.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1.4.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Coordination with repeated to does not by itself establish constituency of a verb and to alone.

correct.text: I'd like to open the gate, but I don't need to.
We plan to check the seal and replace the latch.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Infinitival to combines with a VP
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Infinitival to and prepositional to have overlapping histories and some overlapping distributions. A to-infinitival and a to PP nevertheless have distinct syntactic behavior.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1.4.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: An infinitival generally cannot take the same position after another preposition as an NP or gerund-participial can.

correct.text: She agreed to leave.
She agreed to the revised schedule.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: The chapter analyzes to as a VP marker rather than the head verb. Its restriction to subordinate clauses supports this analysis despite some similarities to auxiliaries.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1.4.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: To can be stranded by ellipsis or follow a clause-internal dependent such as not. These properties differ from those of typical clause subordinators.

correct.text: I asked them always to check the seal.
She promised not to disturb the neighbors.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Bare infinitivals and rare overt subjects
statement: Bare infinitivals lack the markers to and for and are usually subjectless. Overt subjects occur in certain polar echoes and rather than complements.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1.4.3 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The echo is informal and favors accusative pronouns. The rather than construction with a subject is rare.

correct.text: She could check the valve.
Me check the valve? Surely not.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Bare infinitivals and rare overt subjects
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Verb, noun and adjective forms ending in ing
statement: An ing form can be a gerund-participle of a verb, a gerundial noun or a participial adjective. Dependents and clause function help distinguish them.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1.5 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The traditional gerund and present participle labels do not identify different verbal inflections in this analysis.

correct.text: We discussed closing the road.
The gradual closing of the road surprised us.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Verb, noun and adjective forms ending in ing
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Gerund-participials occur as complements, modifiers and supplements. They can resemble NPs in distribution while differing in extraposition and internal syntax.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1.5 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Extraposition judgments vary. Existential there permits some hybrid no constructions, while other mixed nominal and verbal dependents are marginal.

correct.text: Closing the gate was sensible.
It was sensible closing the gate.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A genitive before a verbal ing form can be the clause subject. Verbal dependents and the possibility of omission support this analysis.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1.5 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Subject omission can change who is understood to perform the action. In an NP, a genitive can instead function as determiner.

correct.text: I regretted her leaving the firm.
I regretted leaving the firm.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Initial subjects and comparison with for
statement: A gerund-participial subject comes first, whether genitive or non-genitive. Infinitival for is a separate marker, whereas the gerund-participial genitive is a case form.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1.5 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The genitive is not available for all NPs, and non-genitive subjects are allowed in many gerund-participial complements.

correct.text: I remember their leaving at dawn.
I remember them leaving at dawn.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Initial subjects and comparison with for
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A supplementary gerund-participial can have a nominative pronoun or plain-case NP subject. The nominative construction is relatively formal.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1.6 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Accusative pronouns in this environment are marginal for some speakers. This pattern differs from ordinary complement gerund-participials.

correct.text: She being unavailable, we postponed the interview.
The foreman being unavailable, we postponed the inspection.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Both genitive and non-genitive subjects occur in gerund-participial complements. Formality, NP complexity and the governing construction influence the choice.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1.6 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: A matrix object does not take genitive case merely because a gerund-participial follows it. A nominal determiner is a separate construction.

correct.text: I remember his reading the minutes aloud.
I remember him reading the minutes aloud.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Controlled, raised and contextually inferred subjects
statement: An understood non-finite subject can be controlled by an antecedent, interpreted through raising, or recovered from discourse without a syntactically specified antecedent.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1.7 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: A raised NP has its semantic role in the lower clause, as in Mina seemed to finish the audit.

correct.text: Mina tried to finish the audit.
It is more comfortable to travel by train.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Controlled, raised and contextually inferred subjects
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Ordinary and raised subjects of infinitival catenatives
statement: An ordinary subject supplies an argument of the matrix verb and can control the infinitival subject. A raised subject has its semantic role in the infinitival alone.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §2.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: A finite paraphrase can expose the distinction when the matrix verb allows a finite complement.

correct.text: Mina hoped to finish the audit.
Mina seemed to finish the audit.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Ordinary and raised subjects of infinitival catenatives
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Changing the lower clause from active to passive can preserve propositional meaning with a raising verb. With a non-raising verb the changed matrix subject can alter who holds the attitude.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §2.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Differences in discourse prominence can remain even when propositional content is equivalent.

correct.text: The dog seemed to frighten the visitors.
The visitors seemed to be frightened by the dog.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Selection and dummy subjects in raising
statement: A raised subject need only satisfy the lower predicate's selection restrictions. A dummy there or it is possible if licensed in the lower clause.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §2.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: A referential it with an independently established antecedent is not a dummy.

correct.text: There seemed to be a delay.
It seemed to be raining.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Selection and dummy subjects in raising
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Complement and passive diagnostics for subject raising
statement: A non-raising verb can allow an active complex counterpart or an extraposed passive. For the infinitival raising verbs under comparison, the simple construction is the available catenative pattern.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §2.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Lack of a complex or passive counterpart does not by itself establish raising. The finite complement diagnostic is unavailable if a verb lacks such complements.

correct.text: We arranged for the ferry to leave early.
It was hoped to reopen the pier by noon.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Complement and passive diagnostics for subject raising
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Aspectual begin allows dummy subjects and voice-neutral contrasts. Apparent agency with a particular subject can arise from the predicate and context without requiring a separate agent argument of begin.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §2.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Active and passive versions can differ in naturalness. A context that makes the activity intentional does not by itself settle raising.

correct.text: There began to be a problem with the alarm.
Nina began to unwrap the parcel.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Ordinary and raised subjects with gerund-participials
statement: The ordinary-versus-raised distinction also applies to simple gerund-participial catenatives. Enjoy assigns a role to its subject, while aspectual keep does not impose an independent subject role.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §2.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Finite paraphrases are less widely available than with infinitivals, so voice, selection and dummy subjects are important evidence.

correct.text: Mara enjoyed reading to the children.
There kept being interruptions.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Ordinary and raised subjects with gerund-participials
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Simple and complex alternation with gerund-participials
statement: Some verbs allow both a simple and a complex gerund-participial construction. The semantic effect of adding an intervening NP depends on the verb.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §2.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Complex keep can add a causative interpretation. With like, the matrix experiencer remains the same across the simple and complex patterns.

correct.text: Omar kept waiting outside.
Omar kept us waiting outside.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Simple and complex alternation with gerund-participials
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Gerund-participial complements seldom promote in a matrix passive. Some non-raising verbs allow it, especially where the understood subject need not be the matrix subject.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §2.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Acceptability varies with the lexical head and context. Promotion does not by itself establish ordinary NP-object status.

correct.text: Walking alone at night is not recommended.
Parking on the verge was discouraged.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A gerund-participial complement of certain verbs can have a passive interpretation without overt passive marking.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §2.3 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: An ing expression can also have a nominal analysis. Want with the meaning need has a variety-sensitive distribution.

correct.text: The fence needs painting.
The application requires checking.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A concealed passive has a passive interpretation. A hollow clause is active and has an understood non-subject element linked elsewhere in the construction.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §2.3 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Worth permits a hollow construction rather than the concealed passive pattern. Some verbs admit both patterns with different complementation.

correct.text: The report needs reviewing.
The report is worth reviewing.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Ordinary and raised objects of plain-complex infinitivals
statement: In the plain-complex infinitival construction the intervening NP is a matrix object. Its semantic role can be associated with the matrix verb, or solely with the infinitival.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.1.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Persuade assigns a persuadee role, whereas the intended situation supplies Jo's role in the second example.

correct.text: Mina persuaded Jo to interview the finalist.
Mina intended Jo to interview the finalist.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Ordinary and raised objects of plain-complex infinitivals
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Voice and selection diagnostics for object raising
statement: A raised object can change with the lower clause's voice while the intended situation remains equivalent. A non-raised object is independently selected by the matrix predicate.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.1.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Changing the object of persuade would also change whom the persuasion targeted. Metaphorical uses can extend selection.

correct.text: Mina intended Jo to inspect the latch.
Mina intended the latch to be inspected by Jo.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Voice and selection diagnostics for object raising
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Dummy objects and optional intervening NPs
statement: Dummy objects can occur with raised-object verbs if the infinitival licenses them. Some raised-object verbs also allow a simple construction when the understood subject is coreferential.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.1.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Believe can require the intervening object even with coreference. The absence of a simple alternative does not exclude raising.

correct.text: They intended there to be a break.
I intended to leave before sunset.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Dummy objects and optional intervening NPs
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Subject interpretation in the for-complex construction
statement: For introduces an overt infinitival subject in the complex construction. A corresponding simple construction can have a subjectless infinitival controlled by the matrix subject.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.1.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Verbs vary in whether they allow both constructions. Related patterns with the same verb can differ in meaning or complementation.

correct.text: I arranged for her to travel by rail.
I arranged to travel by rail.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Subject interpretation in the for-complex construction
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A selected prepositional complement can contain an NP controlling the understood subject of a separate infinitival complement.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.1.3 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The controller has an independent role. The construction does not license existential dummy there as that oblique controller.

correct.text: She relied on him to lock the shop.
I signaled to her to stop.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Ordinary objects and subordinate subjects with gerund-participials
statement: Catch can have a matrix object controlling a gerund-participial. With resent the preceding NP is instead the subject of the gerund-participial complement.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.2.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The first NP can promote in a matrix passive. The second can be genitive and forms a constituent with the following VP.

correct.text: We caught Mina reading the log.
We resented Mina's reading the log.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Ordinary objects and subordinate subjects with gerund-participials
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Catenative see can take a syntactic matrix object that is semantically an argument of the following gerund-participial alone.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.2.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The relevant NP cannot take genitive case. A gerund-participial adjunct with see has a distinct analysis.

correct.text: I saw the storm approaching.
The storm was seen approaching.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A concealed passive can occur with an intervening NP interpreted as the affected participant in the lower situation.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.2.3 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The complex pattern is variety-sensitive. Genitive marking of the whole intervening NP is unavailable in this construction.

correct.text: She needs her coat mending.
The manager wants the locks changing.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Catenative complements as a distinct function
statement: Similarities between an NP complement and a non-finite clause do not establish identical functions. The chapter distinguishes catenative complements from objects and predicatives.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Some non-finite clauses do have familiar functions, such as subject or predicative complement, in non-catenative constructions.

correct.text: They remembered the address.
They remembered to check the address.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Catenative complements as a distinct function
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Limits of object, oblique and predicative analogies
statement: Object–oblique contrasts with NPs and object–predicative contrasts with NPs or AdjPs do not systematically extend to catenative infinitivals.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: A matrix verb can license both a predicative and a catenative complement. That alternation does not establish that they have the same function.

correct.text: She seems calm.
She seems to understand the instructions.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Limits of object, oblique and predicative analogies
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Promotion, pronoun substitution, interrogative what and clefts provide uneven evidence that a catenative complement resembles an NP object.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Some gerund-participials promote, and a few infinitivals occur in extraposed passive patterns. Neither result generalizes to the whole class.

correct.text: Leaving without notice was not recommended.
It was planned to move the office in June.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Core and non-core uses of auxiliaries
statement: An auxiliary in core use combines with a following non-finite verb. Some auxiliaries have additional uses with a different complement structure.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Auxiliary status in the chapter depends on negation, inversion, code and emphasis. A core use can also occur with its complement omitted by ellipsis.

correct.text: The door is opening.
The door is open.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Core and non-core uses of auxiliaries
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Overt object with active believe plus an infinitival
statement: In the active believe construction with a to-infinitival complement, an intervening matrix object is required, including when it refers to the matrix subject.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.1.1 of Chapter 14.
violation: An active believe clause takes a to-infinitival without the required intervening object.

exceptions.description: The corresponding passive has no intervening object. Believe also takes finite complements, and other catenative verbs allow subject-controlled infinitivals.

correct.text: Nina believed herself to be qualified.
I believed myself to be ready.

incorrect.text: Nina believed to be qualified.
I believed to be ready.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Overt object with active believe plus an infinitival
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

diagnostic.error_pattern: An active believe clause takes a to-infinitival without the required intervening object.
minimal_pairs: Nina believed to be qualified. ||| Nina believed herself to be qualified.
I believed to be ready. ||| I believed myself to be ready.
diagnostic.learner_explanation: In the active believe construction with a to-infinitival complement, an intervening matrix object is required, including when it refers to the matrix subject.
diagnostic.corrected_paragraph_template: Supply an object, using a reflexive when the object refers back to the matrix subject.
false_positive_guards: Nina was believed to be qualified.
I believed that I was ready.
Nina hoped to be qualified.

statement: Coordinated main clauses can independently vary polarity and retain their main-clause status. A subordinate complement contributes to a larger utterance and has a more restricted range of clause types.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.2.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Whether a closed interrogative complement is available can depend on the polarity or clause type of the matrix.

correct.text: Maya checked the meter, but Jo didn't record it.
Maya said that Jo didn't record it.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A non-finite complement lacks inflectional tense and often leaves its subject and time interpretation to the governing construction or context.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.2.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Loss of some independent options is compatible with clause status.

correct.text: Mara said that she opened the gate yesterday.
Mara asked to open the gate after lunch.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: The dependent-auxiliary proposal treats a core auxiliary as a dependent in a verbal group headed by the lexical verb. It appeals to the close integration of auxiliary and following verb.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.2.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: This is the competing analysis considered in the chapter. The chapter ultimately adopts the catenative analysis.

correct.text: The crew had repaired the lift.
The lift had been repaired by the crew.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Non-argument subjects of auxiliaries and lexical raising verbs
statement: Core auxiliaries need not assign an independent semantic role to the subject. Lexical raising verbs show the same property, so subject selection alone does not justify a separate auxiliary structure.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.2.1–4.2.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Voice neutrality and the availability of dummy subjects help diagnose the shared property.

correct.text: There had been an error.
There seemed to be an error.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Non-argument subjects of auxiliaries and lexical raising verbs

concept: Syntactic negation versus scope with modals
statement: The same syntactic pattern of modal plus not can have different scope relations. Negation may apply to the modal meaning or occur within its scope.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.2.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: With the permission reading of may, the first denies permission. The second imposes a requirement to refrain.

correct.text: You may not open the panel yet.
You must not open the panel yet.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Syntactic negation versus scope with modals
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A perfect following a modal can locate the modalized event before the orientation time or contribute to a past-oriented modal judgment. The order stays the same.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.2.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Some combinations are ambiguous in context. The scope relations do not require a reversal of surface order.

correct.text: I may have left it in the van.
I should have checked the latch yesterday.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Placement and interpretation of frequency adjuncts
statement: The syntactic position of a frequency adjunct and the predicate it qualifies semantically need not coincide in a modal construction.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.2.1–4.2.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: With epistemic must, a reading can associate frequency with the checking, even when the adjunct precedes must.

correct.text: He must always have checked the locks.
He always must have checked the locks.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Placement and interpretation of frequency adjuncts
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Auxiliary uses and lexical raising parallels
statement: The catenative analysis groups core auxiliary uses with lexical catenatives, allowing them to select a non-finite complement. Subject relations and certain non-core uses support treating the auxiliary as a head.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.2.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Special uses of dare and would rather provide further evidence against treating auxiliaries uniformly as dependents.

correct.text: She had finished the inspection.
She seemed to have finished the inspection.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Auxiliary uses and lexical raising parallels
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Primary and secondary negation with auxiliaries
statement: A negative can apply to the auxiliary clause or to its lower non-finite complement. Some constructions allow both.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.2.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: A reversed-polarity tag can distinguish matrix negation from lower negation. Double negation of the two levels is relatively uncommon.

correct.text: She can't always answer the phone, can she?
She can always not answer the phone, can't she?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Primary and secondary negation with auxiliaries
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Some catenatives permit distinct time specifications for the matrix and lower events, while others tightly integrate their times. Auxiliary constructions can also distinguish an orientation time from an event time.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.2.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: A fronted time adjunct tends to specify the higher time or time of orientation. Lexical selection constrains separate time specifications.

correct.text: This morning Jo promised to return tonight.
When Jo called, the crew had already left.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Preposing and coordination can treat the lexical VP with its complements as a constituent excluding the auxiliary. An adjunct can also intervene between the auxiliary and that VP.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.2.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Not all coordination is diagnostic. Delayed right constituent coordination can produce apparent counterexamples.

correct.text: She said he'd be repairing the gate, and repairing the gate he was.
You can't join the choir and not sing.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Auxiliary order under the catenative analysis
statement: In the catenative analysis the order of core auxiliaries follows from their form and selection restrictions. A modal heads the chain, and passive be immediately precedes the passivized verb.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.2.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The second example is grammatically possible but stylistically heavy. Have to can appear on either side of perfect have because its have is not a modal auxiliary.

correct.text: The report may have been revised.
The report has been being revised.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Auxiliary order under the catenative analysis
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: In a core auxiliary chain expressing both perfect and progressive, perfect have precedes progressive be.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.2.1–4.2.2 of Chapter 14.
violation: Progressive be precedes perfect have in a core chain intended to express perfect progressive aspect.

exceptions.description: The constraint applies to core perfect have and progressive be in one chain. Lexical having and separate clauses have different structures.

correct.text: She has been checking the seals.
They have been inspecting the roof.

incorrect.text: She is having checked the seals.
They are having inspected the roof.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

diagnostic.error_pattern: Progressive be precedes perfect have in a core chain intended to express perfect progressive aspect.
minimal_pairs: She is having checked the seals. ||| She has been checking the seals.
They are having inspected the roof. ||| They have been inspecting the roof.
diagnostic.learner_explanation: In a core auxiliary chain expressing both perfect and progressive, perfect have precedes progressive be.
diagnostic.corrected_paragraph_template: Use finite perfect have followed by been and the gerund-participle.
false_positive_guards: She is having the seals checked.
They have inspected the roof.
They are inspecting the roof.
