concept: Case variation and traditional ing categories
statement: Subject case distinguishes certain complement and supplementary gerund-participials. Subjectless constructions supply no comparable internal case evidence for splitting the verbal inflection.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.3 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Non-genitive case is also possible in many complements. A supplementary nominative is relatively formal.

correct.text: She resented his being selected first.
He being the only volunteer, we asked him to start.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Case variation and traditional ing categories
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Limits of noun and adjective analogies for gerund-participials
statement: Alternation with an NP or AdjP does not consistently divide gerund-participial complements into object-like and predicative classes. Related aspectual verbs can license different non-clausal dependents.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.3 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The comparison concerns verbal ing clauses. A gerundial noun and a participial adjective remain separate categories.

correct.text: He kept checking the gauges.
He stopped checking the gauges.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Limits of noun and adjective analogies for gerund-participials
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Aspect does not separate the traditional ing categories
statement: Whether an ing clause receives a progressive interpretation depends on the construction and context. It does not consistently track the traditional gerund and present-participle labels.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.3 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The ing inflection alone does not establish progressive aspect.

correct.text: We saw Jo repairing the latch.
Jo began repairing the latch.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Aspect does not separate the traditional ing categories
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A purpose adjunct can often take in order and move to the front. A selected infinitival complement instead supplies content licensed by its governing verb.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.4 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: With some verbs a string permits both readings. Prosody, punctuation and lexical meaning can affect the interpretation.

correct.text: In order to impress the panel, she rehearsed.
She promised to impress the panel.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Purpose and complementation with motion verbs
statement: A to-infinitival following a motion verb can resemble a purpose adjunct but have a tighter semantic relation with the verb. Some uses of be or move license a complement rather than an optional purpose specification.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.4 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: With go, wait and hurry the boundary can be less sharp. Availability of a purpose paraphrase alone is not decisive.

correct.text: Mina has been to see the new exhibition.
The council moved to address the complaints.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Purpose and complementation with motion verbs
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Result and cause adjuncts versus complements
statement: An infinitival may describe an optional result or cause, or may be licensed as a complement in a particular sense of a verb.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.4 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Omission and coordination paraphrases can help. Omission may leave a grammatical sentence while changing the matrix sense.

correct.text: I ran to the platform, only to find it empty.
She lived to see the bridge reopen.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Result and cause adjuncts versus complements
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A gerund-participial can depict a concurrent state or activity. With certain motion and posture verbs the boundary between adjunct and complement can be less clear.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.4 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Adding a locative can make an adjunct more readily omissible in a posture construction.

correct.text: He came in smiling broadly.
She sat on the patio reading the newspaper.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Try and and plain-form go constructions
statement: The chapter analyzes the and phrase after try in the illustrated use as a non-finite complement. A restricted go construction permits a following plain verb without and.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.4 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Ordinary coordination with go and occurs more widely. In the no-and construction both verbs are plain forms.

correct.text: Try and keep the door closed.
Go get the spare key.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Try and and plain-form go constructions
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Catenative verbs are classified by simple or complex complementation, complement form and syntactic diagnostics. Distinct senses of a verb may require separate entries.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: In the examples, try means endeavor with the infinitival and test a method with the gerund-participial. Some verbs alternate without that change of sense.

correct.text: They tried to free the latch.
They tried pressing the latch sideways.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Passive classification distinguishes promotion of an intervening NP, extraposition of an infinitival, and promotion of a gerund-participial.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: These patterns have different distributions. Some verbs require or block a particular passive, and finite alternants and other complement options are recorded separately.

correct.text: She was advised to wait.
Waiting outside was not recommended.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Some catenatives have a finite declarative alternant or near-alternant. Its form can be unmodalized or include a modal preterite, will, a mandative, or should.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: With some predicates the finite alternative changes the interpretation. The finite pattern has to be established for each lexical sense.

correct.text: They demanded to speak first.
They demanded that they speak first.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Modal auxiliaries, supportive do and some modal idioms take bare infinitival complements in the simple construction.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Dare and would rather differ from the general raised-subject pattern. Auxiliary dare and lexical dare have different distributions.

correct.text: The ferry might leave early.
Did the ferry leave early?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Ordinary and raised subjects in simple-only to-infinitivals
statement: Simple-only to-infinitival verbs include ordinary-subject predicates such as decide and raising predicates such as seem. Different senses of one verb can belong to different classes.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The second threat is a prediction of an unwelcome possibility. Some verbs show marginal complex alternatives or mixed raising diagnostics.

correct.text: Mina decided to stay.
The storm threatened to intensify.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Ordinary and raised subjects in simple-only to-infinitivals
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Some simple-only catenatives permit both a to-infinitival and a gerund-participial, while others select only a participial form. Subject interpretation is a separate dimension.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Aspectual begin differs from ordinary-subject avoid. Perfect have and passive be and get take past-participials in the simple construction.

correct.text: The child began to laugh.
The child began laughing.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Simple and complex variants within a lexical sense
statement: Class 2 requires a simple and complex use with the same catenative sense. In the simple construction the understood lower subject may be controlled or left to context.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.3 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Simple help and say can involve contextual interpretation. With help the inferred participant may be less salient than the matrix subject.

correct.text: She asked to leave.
She asked Omar to leave.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Simple and complex variants within a lexical sense
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Object and subject control with promise and ask
statement: An overt object generally controls the lower subject in ordinary-object catenatives, but particular verbs and complement meanings can support subject control.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.3 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: With the permission reading of the second sentence, Mina is the prospective leaver. Promise with an intervening object and an infinitival is marginal for many speakers.

correct.text: Mina promised to call at noon.
Mina asked Jo to be allowed to leave.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Object and subject control with promise and ask
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An infinitival after pay can describe the action the payee is to perform or the purpose of the payer's expenditure.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.3 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The second reading is near the boundary between a selected complement and a purpose adjunct.

correct.text: They paid her to repair the gate.
They paid her to watch her repair the gate.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Some verbs alternate between simple and for-complex infinitivals, while others take a selected oblique whose referent can remain understood.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.3 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The oblique interpretation can be recoverable in a simple-looking form. A corresponding for PP with an NP is not available for every verb that permits the clause.

correct.text: They hoped for Mina to attend.
She signaled to us to stop.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Liking verbs with both main complement forms
statement: Several liking and disliking predicates permit infinitivals and gerund-participials in simple and complex constructions. In the gerund-participial, some permit a genitive subject.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.3 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Genitives tend to be formal. Detest and most uses of dislike select gerund-participials.

correct.text: I hate wasting time.
I hate his interrupting the meeting.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Liking verbs with both main complement forms
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Concealed passives and asymmetric form choices
statement: A verb can allow both major form types without licensing them in the same simple and complex environments. Need can take a concealed passive, while intend allows a gerund-participial in its simple pattern.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.3 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The complex intend pattern uses the infinitival. Want meaning need differs from want expressing desire.

correct.text: The jacket needs mending.
I intended reading the report before lunch.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Concealed passives and asymmetric form choices
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A complex gerund-participial with want can describe an ongoing situation, but in a non-affirmative context it can have a non-progressive reading.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.3 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The second can prohibit bringing food at all. The progressive interpretation is not obligatory.

correct.text: I want them standing when the curtain rises.
I don't want you bringing food into the lab.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Controlled and contextual subjects with gerund-participials
statement: A simple gerund-participial can have a matrix-controlled subject or a contextually inferred subject, depending on the governing verb and sense.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.3 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Complex alternants can make the lower subject explicit. Some verbs in this grouping also select infinitivals in particular environments.

correct.text: I remember buying the tickets.
I wouldn't recommend buying the tickets.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Controlled and contextual subjects with gerund-participials
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Complex-only ordinary and raised infinitival objects
statement: Complex-only infinitival catenatives include predicates with ordinary matrix objects and predicates with raised objects. Cognition and saying verbs often have the raised pattern.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.4 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Some saying predicates strongly favor or require the matrix passive in this construction. Different lexical senses can have different distributions.

correct.text: She persuaded Jo to wait.
They believed Jo to be waiting.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Complex-only ordinary and raised infinitival objects
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Infinitival marker in passive causative make
statement: Causative make takes a bare infinitival after its object in the active and a to-infinitival in the corresponding passive.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.4 of Chapter 14.
violation: The infinitival marker is added in active causative make or omitted in its passive counterpart.

exceptions.description: The alternation concerns causative make. Do not extend it to lexical make with an NP or to other causative verbs.

correct.text: They made us wait outside.
We were made to wait outside.

incorrect.text: They made us to wait outside.
We were made wait outside.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Infinitival marker in passive causative make
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

diagnostic.error_pattern: The infinitival marker is added in active causative make or omitted in its passive counterpart.
minimal_pairs: They made us to wait outside. ||| They made us wait outside.
We were made wait outside. ||| We were made to wait outside.
diagnostic.learner_explanation: Causative make takes a bare infinitival after its object in the active and a to-infinitival in the corresponding passive.
diagnostic.corrected_paragraph_template: Use the bare infinitival in the active and add to in the corresponding passive.

concept: Permission and ordering with raised objects
statement: With some permission and ordering predicates, the object can belong semantically only to the authorized or ordered situation.

exceptions.description: A human object may be interpreted as the recipient of permission or an order in context. The syntax does not always encode that role.

correct.text: They allowed the gate to remain open.
The director ordered the meeting to resume.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Permission and ordering with raised objects
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Force and compel typically assign a role to the object. Cause and enable can take raised objects, while make and get show a more varied pattern.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.4 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Dummy objects, voice and selection can point in different directions for some causatives. Past-participial get is not simply the passive infinitival alternant of every get construction.

The fault caused the lights to fail.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Complex-only obliques and multiple form types
statement: Some complex-only infinitival constructions require a selected oblique. Other complex-only verbs, including causatives and perception verbs, license several non-finite forms.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.4 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The complement inventory and possibility of matrix passivization depend on the verb and construction.

correct.text: They appealed to us to reopen the hall.
She had the lock repaired.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Complex-only obliques and multiple form types
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Sensory perception verbs can take a bare infinitival to present an event as a whole or a gerund-participial to present it in progress.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.4 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: A past-participial can express passive meaning. Active inferential see with a to-infinitival differs from ordinary sensory see.

correct.text: I saw the cyclist cross the bridge.
I saw the cyclist crossing the bridge.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A matrix passive with see can license a to-infinitival where active sensory see takes a bare infinitival. The passive can carry an inferential component.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.4 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The alternatives are not automatically identical in meaning. Perfect infinitivals can occur with the inferential use.

correct.text: The witness was seen to leave the building.
They saw the witness leave the building.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Some complex gerund-participials allow a genitive subject and have a prepositional alternant with for or from.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.4 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Stop varies with sense and normally resists a genitive in this construction. The prepositional version often has different passive possibilities.

correct.text: Forgive my interrupting the meeting.
Forgive me for interrupting the meeting.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Causative and perception gerund-participials without genitive
statement: Other complex gerund-participials exclude a genitive preceding NP. They include uses of aspectual causatives, perception predicates and discovery predicates.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.4 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: They do not all have the same raising or passive behavior. Imagine-like see has a distinct pattern from sensory see.

correct.text: The delay kept us waiting.
We caught Jo copying the key.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Causative and perception gerund-participials without genitive
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: The chapter indexes catenative verbs and idioms by construction class and distinguishes senses where complementation changes.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.5 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The index consolidates the preceding classifications. A listed sense should not be generalized to all uses of a verb.

correct.text: They kept waiting by the gate.
They kept us waiting by the gate.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Lexical selection and meaning tendencies by form
statement: Complement form must be established lexically. To-infinitivals are often associated with projected or potential events, and gerund-participials with actual or current events.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.6.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: These associations do not determine selection or apply in every use.

correct.text: She promised to call after lunch.
She enjoyed talking with the crew.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Lexical selection and meaning tendencies by form
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Some aspectual verbs permit both major forms with little difference. In other contexts the infinitival can favor onset and the gerund-participial ongoing activity.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.6.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Some states and existential patterns favor the infinitival. An interpretation involving activity already under way can favor the gerund-participial.

correct.text: It started to rain.
It started raining.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Form preferences with liking and memory
statement: An infinitival can favor an intended or projected activity, while a gerund-participial can describe an actual state or remembered event.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.6.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Would like strongly favors an infinitival in requests or intentions, while liking an existing state often favors a gerund-participial.

correct.text: I remembered to lock the gate.
I remembered locking the gate.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Form preferences with liking and memory
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Aspectual and lexical contrasts across form types
statement: A form alternation can contrast attainment with ongoing activity or distinguish lexical readings such as attempting and testing a method.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.6.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: With try, fear, scorn, regret and report, the form contrast can involve different semantic factors.

correct.text: I finally got the pump to work.
I finally got the pump working.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

statement: Some progressive catenatives resist a following gerund-participial complement, particularly aspectual verbs and some verbs taking concealed passives.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.6.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: This restriction is lexical and speaker judgments vary. Successive verbal ing forms are possible with many other catenatives.

correct.text: It was starting to rain.
We were considering buying a new pump.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Selection and variation in bare infinitivals
statement: Bare infinitivals are selected by a limited group including core modals and certain causative and perception verbs. Some other verbs allow a bare form in restricted environments.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.6.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The second is characteristic of British English; American English uses to. Some speakers distinguish readings of help by the form selected.

correct.text: We helped Jo lift the crate.
I'd never known Jo lose her temper before.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Selection and variation in bare infinitivals
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Past-participial catenative complements occur with perfect have, passive auxiliaries and some lexical verbs. Complex lexical examples commonly express passive meaning.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.6.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Some alternate with passive infinitivals, while others occur in concealed passive or variety-sensitive constructions.

correct.text: We heard the window smashed.
She had the lock replaced.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Missing elements in hollow non-finite clauses
statement: A hollow non-finite clause has an understood non-subject element recoverable from an antecedent. The missing element is commonly a verb object or preposition complement.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The object of the verb is missing in the first and the preposition complement in the second. Other gap functions are more restricted.

correct.text: This piece is hard to play on a flute.
This flute is hard to play that piece on.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Missing elements in hollow non-finite clauses
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Worth and worthwhile and purposive for can license a gerund-participial with an understood object or preposition complement.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.1–6.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: With worth the subordinate subject is typically generic. Bear in some negative expressions can also take a hollow complement.

correct.text: The proposal is worth looking into.
The jar is for storing nails in.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Hollow complements of predicative adjectives and nouns
statement: An adjective or predicative noun can license a hollow infinitival whose gap is interpreted from the higher subject.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.3 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Some heads also allow an ordinary infinitival as subject or extraposed subject, while others are collocationally restricted.

correct.text: The latch is awkward to reach.
The lecture was a pleasure to listen to.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Hollow complements of predicative adjectives and nouns
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: The higher subject in a hollow construction is independently related to the higher predicate. Unlike raised subjects, it cannot be a dummy licensed solely by the lower predicate.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.3 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: A hollow construction and an extraposed-subject construction can differ in meaning even when both are available.

correct.text: The report is hard to verify.
There seems to be a discrepancy.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Optional gaps with ready and similar adjectives
statement: An adjective such as ready can license a hollow infinitival with an understood object or an ordinary infinitival with an understood subject linked to the higher subject.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.3 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Context can allow both readings for some higher subjects.

correct.text: The forms are ready to file.
The clerk is ready to file the forms.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Optional gaps with ready and similar adjectives
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Hollow infinitivals licensed by attributive adjectives
statement: A hollow infinitival inside an NP can be licensed indirectly by an attributive adjective, which evaluates the action involving the noun referent.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.3 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The string may also permit a relative-clause reading. A relative often conveys possibility or suitability, whereas the adjective-licensed construction can describe an actual event.

correct.text: It was a difficult latch to replace.
That is an easy trail to get lost on.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Hollow infinitivals licensed by attributive adjectives
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Be and a small group of transitive verbs can license hollow infinitivals. With cost or take the construction can include a measure expression.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.3 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The missing lower element is interpreted from an antecedent in the higher construction. Related ordinary or passive alternatives depend on the verb.

correct.text: The cabinet took an hour to assemble.
That decision is for you to make.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Hollow infinitivals with adjectives, degree items and purpose
statement: A hollow gap can occur with some postpositive adjective constructions, in degree complements and in purpose infinitivals.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.3 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Degree and purpose constructions also permit ordinary infinitivals without a non-subject gap.

correct.text: The soup is too hot to serve.
I bought this box to keep the cables in.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Hollow infinitivals with adjectives, degree items and purpose
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Non-finites can function as subjects, objects or predicative complements independently of the catenative function.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Progressive, passive and quasi-modal uses of be instead take catenative complements. Some complex-transitive cases require lexical analysis.

correct.text: To ignore the warning would be foolish.
Their main goal was to reduce delays.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An infinitival subject or extraposed subject commonly presents a situation, while a non-mandative finite counterpart can present a proposition or fact.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The difference can be slight with mandatives. Predicates evaluating truth need not accept the infinitival counterpart.

correct.text: It was good to see them again.
It was good that they arrived safely.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Actuality and extraposition of non-finite subjects
statement: Infinitival subjects often present potential situations and extrapose readily. Gerund-participial subjects also allow hypothetical interpretations, but are more restricted in some extraposed and overt-subject contexts.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Subject position, predicate choice and actuality affect the comparison. Bare infinitival subjects are restricted.

correct.text: It would be better for the hearing to be postponed.
Changing the date would cause problems.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Actuality and extraposition of non-finite subjects
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A non-finite can function as an object in a complex-transitive construction or as an extraposed object with a dummy it in object position.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: To-infinitivals do not normally occur in the object position before a predicative complement. The range of gerund-participial extraposed objects is more restricted.

correct.text: I found working at night exhausting.
I found it exhausting to work at night.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Specifying be can take a to-infinitival, bare infinitival or gerund-participial predicative complement. A to-infinitival can also describe purpose.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.3 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The bare form is restricted by the subject construction. Some gerund-participials are ambiguous with progressive be.

correct.text: All I did was tighten the latch.
The barrier is to keep the animals inside.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Direct adjective complements and neighboring functions
statement: A directly selected infinitival is distinct from an indirect degree complement, a clause adjunct or an extraposed subject.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §8.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: An evaluative adjunct can indicate how an action reflects on the subject. An extraposed subject falls outside the adjective phrase.

correct.text: Jo was eager to leave.
Jo was too tired to leave.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Direct adjective complements and neighboring functions
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Adjectives such as likely permit a raised subject with no independent semantic role, while adjectives such as determined assign a role to the higher subject.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §8.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Voice neutrality and dummy subjects are useful together. Able can give equivalent active and passive propositions without requiring a raising analysis.

correct.text: There is likely to be a delay.
Jo was determined to finish.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Busy can take an ordinary gerund-participial directly. Worth and worthwhile can take hollow complements and also occur with ordinary complements in impersonal patterns.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §8.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Other adjectives can take gerund-participials through a selected preposition, as in keen on.

correct.text: She was busy sorting the files.
The file is worth keeping.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Some nouns select infinitivals, including subjectless and, where licensed, for-subject variants. The noun's selection need not match that of a related verb or adjective.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §8.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: A superficially similar infinitival with an adjective can instead function as a clause adjunct.

correct.text: We had an opportunity to inspect the roof.
They sought permission for the gate to be opened.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Nominal complements and absence of raising
statement: An NP dependent of a noun must remain interpretable as an argument of that noun. A separate infinitival subject after for can belong solely to the lower clause.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §8.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: A dummy cannot be used as a genitive or oblique dependent of the noun in the way it can occur as the subject of a for-clause.

correct.text: They discussed the tendency for there to be delays.
They discussed the staff's tendency to arrive early.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Nominal complements and absence of raising
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Gerund-participials are widely available as preposition complements. Infinitivals are more restricted, and some prepositions also admit past-participial or verbless reductions.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §8.3 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Prepositional to in look forward to is distinct from infinitival to. Reduced complements depend on the selecting preposition.

correct.text: We look forward to meeting them.
Although damaged in transit, the crate was usable.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Degree licensors and position of infinitivals
statement: Too, enough and sufficient or sufficiently can license infinitivals that set a threshold for a purpose or requirement.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §8.4 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The infinitival is licensed indirectly. End position is often preferred but is not always possible.

correct.text: It was too late to phone.
Enough volunteers arrived to move the piano.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Degree licensors and position of infinitivals
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Some prepositions take an infinitival licensed by the larger construction. So and such can license as with a purposive or resultative infinitival.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §8.4 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Finite alternatives can be available. The relevant licensor can be a matrix predicate or a degree expression.

correct.text: She stepped aside so as to let us pass.
The prints were so faint as to be illegible.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An infinitival can express an open or closed subordinate question, often concerning what action to take.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §8.5 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Closed infinitivals use whether rather than if in this construction. Some heads admit an infinitival interrogative but have more restricted finite counterparts.

correct.text: They asked whether to wait.
They discussed where to wait.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Nouns can have infinitival relatives and gerund-participial or past-participial modifiers. The participial modifiers lack a relative phrase.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: A passive gerund-participial can express progressive aspect, unlike the corresponding bare passive modifier.

correct.text: The people waiting outside need shelter.
The packages delivered this morning are on the table.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A clause-level infinitival can express purpose or an outcome that becomes apparent afterward.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: These modifiers can resemble selected complements in some environments.

correct.text: She stopped to check the address.
He opened the box to find it empty.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A non-finite supplement can have an overt subject of its own, or lack a subject interpreted from the anchor clause.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The temporal, causal or other relation can be inferred rather than explicitly marked.

correct.text: The rain having stopped, we went outside.
Having checked the map, Jo chose the lower trail.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Supplements anchored to phrases or clauses
statement: A non-finite supplement can elaborate an NP or comment on the proposition expressed by a clause.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Some supplements have a contextually inferred subject rather than an antecedent in the anchor.

correct.text: Jo's proposal, intended to reduce delays, won support.
To be honest, I had expected a different result.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Supplements anchored to phrases or clauses
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Verbless clauses after with and without
statement: With and without can take a verbless clause containing a subject and nonverbal predicate.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §10 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The containing PP can modify an NP or function as a clause adjunct. With and without also take non-finite clauses.

correct.text: They waited with the lights off.
She left without her coat on.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Verbless clauses after with and without
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Reduced clauses after prepositions and verbless supplements
statement: Some prepositions that take finite clauses also license verbless reductions. A verbless clause can also appear as a supplement.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §10 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The reduction can preserve the interpretation of a corresponding clause with be. Condensed and lexicalized constructions have additional restrictions.

correct.text: Though tired, Jo finished the shift.
Her hands cold, Jo went indoors.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Reduced clauses after prepositions and verbless supplements
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Some verbless structures allow a bare singular nominal and can become integrated or lexicalized.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §10 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: An integrated condensed phrase can behave differently from an absolute supplement.

correct.text: Dinner over, the guests left.
She dived head first into the water.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: The understood subject can be associated with raising, syntactically controlled by an antecedent, or inferred without a syntactically specified controller.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §11 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: A salient referent in the surrounding clause can support contextual inference without being a syntactic controller.

correct.text: Jo hoped to finish by noon.
It is pleasant to walk here in spring.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Control and contextual interpretation in clause structure
statement: Control is an anaphoric relation to an antecedent in a constructionally specified position. With contextual interpretation the relevant role may be inferred even without an overt antecedent.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §11 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Semantic factors motivate many control patterns without making the antecedent freely selectable.

correct.text: Jo told Mina to arrange the interviews.
It was a mistake to arrange the interviews so late.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Control and contextual interpretation in clause structure
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Nominal versus verbal patterns of understood subjects
statement: The related noun and verb can differ in how they identify an understood lower subject. Nominal complements may allow either participant or leave the subject to context.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §11 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The second sentence can allow different readings depending on context. A nominal antecedent need not provide a syntactic controller.

correct.text: Jo requested Mina to enter the contest.
We received a request from Jo to enter the contest.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Nominal versus verbal patterns of understood subjects
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Successive complements can contribute separate semantic roles to a participant interpreted in more than one subordinate clause.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §11 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The lower subject is interpreted within a chain rather than assigned all its roles by a single predicate.

correct.text: Jo intended to try to settle the dispute.
Mina promised to try to finish early.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Hollow infinitivals after existential there, have, or with can present a task as required. A predicative genitive can instead express entitlement.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.3 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Some strings permit a relative analysis, but the hollow construction can occur where an integrated relative is unavailable.

correct.text: We have two panels to inspect.
The money was not yours to spend.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: No overt subject in infinitival interrogative complements
statement: The infinitival interrogative complement does not allow an overt subject. The fronted interrogative expression also cannot itself serve as its subject.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §8.5 of Chapter 14.
violation: An overt for-subject occurs inside an infinitival interrogative complement.

exceptions.description: A finite interrogative can have an overt subject or a subject interrogative phrase. An ordinary non-interrogative for-infinitival can also have an overt subject.

correct.text: They discussed which route to take.
She explained how to start the pump.

incorrect.text: They discussed which route for them to take.
She explained how for us to start the pump.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: No overt subject in infinitival interrogative complements
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

diagnostic.error_pattern: An overt for-subject occurs inside an infinitival interrogative complement.
minimal_pairs: They discussed which route for them to take. ||| They discussed which route to take.
She explained how for us to start the pump. ||| She explained how to start the pump.
diagnostic.learner_explanation: The infinitival interrogative complement does not allow an overt subject. The fronted interrogative expression also cannot itself serve as its subject.
diagnostic.corrected_paragraph_template: Omit the overt subject when its reference is recoverable, or use a finite interrogative.
false_positive_guards: They discussed which route they should take.
She arranged for us to start the pump.
She explained who started the pump.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Participial NP modifiers without relative markers
statement: A bare participial modifier does not take who as a relative marker. A finite relative with who and a finite auxiliary is a separate construction.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9 of Chapter 14.
violation: Who precedes a bare gerund-participial modifier without a finite auxiliary.

exceptions.description: Preserve finite relative clauses and integrated infinitival relatives. The restriction concerns bare participial NP modifiers.

correct.text: The people waiting outside need shelter.
The workers repairing the lift need more time.

incorrect.text: The people who waiting outside need shelter.
The workers who repairing the lift need more time.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Participial NP modifiers without relative markers
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

diagnostic.error_pattern: Who precedes a bare gerund-participial modifier without a finite auxiliary.
minimal_pairs: The people who waiting outside need shelter. ||| The people waiting outside need shelter.
The workers who repairing the lift need more time. ||| The workers repairing the lift need more time.
diagnostic.learner_explanation: A bare participial modifier does not take who as a relative marker. A finite relative with who and a finite auxiliary is a separate construction.
diagnostic.corrected_paragraph_template: Remove who for a bare participial modifier, or supply a finite auxiliary for a relative clause.
false_positive_guards: The people who are waiting outside need shelter.
The workers repairing the lift need more time.
We asked who was waiting outside.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A quantified controller supplies the interpretation of a lower subject for each relevant individual. Its quantifier need not be repeated within the subordinate proposition.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §11 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: A lower reflexive can reveal a distributive interpretation.

correct.text: Both runners hope to finish first.
Nobody intends to delay you.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Sentence and clause as distinct units
statement: A sentence can have the form of one clause or a coordination of clauses. A clause can also occur inside another clause.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1 of Chapter 2.

exceptions.description: Sentences are not a separate constituent category in this analysis. Context can also support a non-clausal utterance.

correct.text: The lights went out.
The lights went out, and the crowd fell silent.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Sentence and clause as distinct units
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: The coordinated units can have different syntactic categories when the construction allows them to perform comparable roles.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1 of Chapter 2.

exceptions.description: Coordination does not create a new word class. The analysis depends on the functions of the coordinates.

correct.text: She is a careful driver and very patient.
It was both a surprise and difficult to explain.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: The canonical baseline is positive, declarative, active, main and uncoordinated. A clause can differ on several dimensions at once.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §2 of Chapter 2.

exceptions.description: Canonical describes a syntactic baseline. Non-canonical structures are normal grammatical resources.

correct.text: Mina checked the lock.
Wasn't the lock checked by Mina?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A clause that contains an embedded clause is its matrix. The matrix can itself be subordinate to a higher clause.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §2 of Chapter 2.

exceptions.description: Matrix describes a local embedding relation, whereas main describes the clause's own status.

correct.text: I know that Jo left early.
Mina said that she knew that Jo left early.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A counterpart can differ in a single syntactic dimension while retaining other features. It need not be fully canonical.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §2 of Chapter 2.

exceptions.description: Some non-canonical constructions lack a corresponding clause that differs only on the dimension under comparison.

correct.text: Jo was not called.
Was Jo not called?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A fronted expression can occur outside the clause nucleus and be interpreted in relation to a gap inside it.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §2 of Chapter 2.

exceptions.description: A syntactic process label describes the relationship between constructions rather than a temporal sequence in production.

correct.text: I wonder which latch Jo checked.
That latch, Jo checked twice.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: In the illustrated inversion analysis, the fronted auxiliary is placed in prenuclear position and linked to the corresponding predicator position in the nucleus.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §2 of Chapter 2.

exceptions.description: An inverted auxiliary and a fronted interrogative phrase can both occur in the same clause.

correct.text: Is the latch loose?
Has Jo checked the latch?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Most verbs distinguish primary forms used in finite patterns from secondary forms such as the plain form and participles.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3 of Chapter 2.

exceptions.description: Syncretism can obscure the distinction. Be and modal auxiliaries have special paradigms.

correct.text: She takes the early train.
She has taken the early train.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.2 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Different locatives in a clause need not specify the same spatial relation.

correct.text: We met at the library, in the city centre.
In this town, children usually play outdoors.
