review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Preposition phrases dominate the expression of location. Some prepositions allow no overt complement, and others can describe a static position through an implied endpoint or direction.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.2 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Locative home is restricted to subject-oriented complement use in the construction described here.

correct.text: The crew camped several miles into the woods.
The children played nearby.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A small set of adverbs can express where a situation takes place or the geographic area over which it occurs.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.2 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Preposition phrases are the more general realization of static location.

correct.text: The bakery delivers locally.
The association recruits nationally.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A motion complement can describe the change of location of the subject or the object, depending on which participant moves.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: The same verb can support both orientations in different constructions.

correct.text: Mina rolled into the yard.
Mina rolled the barrel into the yard.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A motion predicate can leave a source or goal unexpressed when its interpretation is recoverable or when the verb makes it predictable.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: The relevant place may come from the situation or the verb's lexical meaning.

correct.text: The guests have already left.
Has the courier arrived?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An endpoint can bound a motion event and license a time-to-completion reading.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: A path phrase may instead describe the route without supplying a final endpoint.

correct.text: The crew sailed for two hours.
The crew sailed to the island in two hours.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Motion inferred from sound or the way construction
statement: A verb of sound can take a motion complement when the sound accompanies inferred movement. The way construction can likewise supply a movement interpretation.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: The construction requires a plausible connection between the verb's event and the movement.

correct.text: A stone clattered down the chute.
We squeezed our way through the crowd.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Motion inferred from sound or the way construction
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Perfect be with a destination can report a completed visit. Perfect go can report departure toward the destination and continued absence.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: The context and variety can affect the interpretation of perfect go.

correct.text: Nia has been to Kyoto twice.
Nia has gone to Kyoto and will return Friday.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Goal marking with where and locative prepositions
statement: Goal to can be omitted with interrogative where. Other location expressions can receive a goal reading from the motion construction itself.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: An unmarked location phrase can also describe where the motion happened.

correct.text: Where did the hikers go?
The dog jumped on the bench.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Goal marking with where and locative prepositions
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: To is the usual explicit goal marker. Into and onto can additionally describe the spatial relation at the endpoint.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Adverbial-looking PPs such as home can express a goal without an overt to.

correct.text: We carried the box to the gate.
The cat leapt onto the railing.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: From commonly marks the source of motion and can take another spatial phrase as its complement.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Out of also marks a source and characterizes it as an interior.

correct.text: The mouse darted from behind the cupboard.
The parcel came from Manila.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A phrase headed by across or through can identify a route or support an endpoint interpretation depending on the motion construction.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: The preposition alone does not settle whether the endpoint is asserted.

correct.text: We drove through the tunnel on our way downtown.
The swimmer made it across the river.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A direction dependent describes the orientation of motion and may leave the eventual destination open.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: A direction phrase can contain a reference place without asserting arrival there.

correct.text: The hikers walked north.
The cart rolled away from the shed.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Constituency of paired source and goal phrases
statement: Source and goal can behave as separate dependents and can also combine into a unit describing a stretch or route.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: In a clause containing both, fronting and the interpretation of a following modifier can help distinguish the analyses.

correct.text: From the depot, the van went to the station.
The trail from the bridge to the summit is steep.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Constituency of paired source and goal phrases
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Spatial source, path and goal expressions extend to ordered abstract domains. Spatial direction and endpoint expressions can also characterize static orientation or topography.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.4 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Static orientation can invoke conceptual movement without describing an actual change of position.

correct.text: The water changed from liquid to vapor.
The cottage faces towards the sea.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Overall extent measures the amount traversed, while terminal-point expressions identify the limits of the stretch.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.1 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: A source or a goal can be overt without an explicit measurement or a second endpoint.

correct.text: The runner covered five kilometres.
The runner went from the gate to the pier.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Spatial extent can measure an actual displacement or the dimensions of a static configuration.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.2 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: A motion-like verb can describe a static configuration without implying a dynamic event.

correct.text: The balloon rose thirty metres.
The fence runs for two kilometres.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Extent can specify distance, height, area or another dimension. Scalar change can use comparable constructions to specify the amount or limits of change.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.2 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Scalar source and goal identify values on a scale rather than positions in physical space.

correct.text: The grounds expanded by two hectares.
The price fell from twelve dollars to nine dollars.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Complement status and bounding of non-temporal extent
statement: Spatial and scalar extent depend on an appropriate predicate and generally behave as complements. A measured change can bound a dynamic situation.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: A measure of a static situation does not produce the same bounding effect.

correct.text: The seedlings grew for six weeks.
The seedlings grew ten centimetres in six weeks.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Complement status and bounding of non-temporal extent
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Extent can be expressed by a measure NP, a PP or a small set of adverb phrases. Spatial and scalar constructions can select different prepositions.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Bare measure phrases are also possible with appropriate predicates.

correct.text: The track stretches for two miles.
The fee increased by five dollars.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A scalar location can assign a value on a scale, while verbs such as cost or weigh can license a measure complement.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.4 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Question patterns and complement properties vary with the predicate and dimension.

correct.text: The membership fee is forty dollars.
The package weighs two kilograms.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Time can be a freely added adjunct or a complement licensed by a predicate. A scheduling predicate can specify the time of its object.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.1 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Friday can locate the interview even when the scheduling happened on another day.

correct.text: I checked the schedule on Monday.
They scheduled the interview for Friday.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Scheduling changes can be described with source and goal expressions parallel to spatial movement.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.1 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: The displaced event or appointment is the theme whose time changes.

correct.text: The hearing moved from Monday to Thursday.
We brought the briefing forward to noon.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A temporal expression can take its reference from utterance time, a calendar convention, or a time supplied by the context.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.2 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: A recurring clock or calendar expression can use a contextual cycle rather than the current one.

correct.text: I arrived yesterday at four.
We first met in 2014.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Time located relative to another situation
statement: An event or interval can serve as the reference point for locating another situation in time.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.2 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: The anchor need not itself have a fixed calendar or clock designation.

correct.text: The power failed during rehearsal.
I called before the inspection.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Time located relative to another situation
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Complement forms in temporal preposition phrases
statement: Temporal prepositions can take noun phrases or clauses, and some also occur without an overt complement.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: The available complement categories depend on the individual preposition.

correct.text: We left after the ceremony.
We left after the guests had eaten.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Complement forms in temporal preposition phrases
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: When and whenever in temporal expressions
statement: When can ask about a time or introduce a time-locating clause, and whenever can leave the time choice open.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Interrogative and temporal-clause uses have different grammatical functions.

correct.text: When will the meeting end?
Take a break whenever you like.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: When and whenever in temporal expressions
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Noun phrases, adverb phrases and some nonfinite clauses can locate a situation in time.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: The temporal relation of a nonfinite clause can depend on inference.

correct.text: We finished last Friday.
Walking to the station, I saw the procession.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A time expression can identify a particular occasion or characterize an occasion without picking out a particular one.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.4 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Seasonal expressions can allow either use depending on context.

correct.text: We met last Sunday.
Have you ever worked on a Sunday?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A temporal clause can identify a time and also suggest a causal connection between the events.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.4 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Temporal linkage alone does not guarantee a causal interpretation.

correct.text: When the fuse blew, the room went dark.
When the bell rang, I was already outside.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A temporal expression may specify a point or an interval. The aspectual reading affects whether the situation is understood to occupy the interval or occur within it.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.4 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: A broad interval such as Monday can locate a brief event without specifying an exact time.

correct.text: The bell rang at noon.
I worked at the library when I lived downtown.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Compatibility of deictic time and tense
statement: A deictic time adjunct and a deictic tense ordinarily agree when they locate the same situation.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.4 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Scheduling, reported speech and shifts of viewpoint can give tense and adjunct different times of application.

correct.text: The parcel arrived yesterday.
The parcel was coming tomorrow, but the delivery was cancelled.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Compatibility of deictic time and tense
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A negative subordinate clause can locate another event when a change of state or a missed expectation supplies an identifiable time.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.4 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: A bare absence with no salient boundary or expected occasion may fail to establish a usable reference time.

correct.text: When the signal no longer flashed, we restarted the machine.
When the courier did not arrive, we called dispatch.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Spatial and temporal extent can identify start and end points or measure the total span.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.1 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Temporal extent has domain-specific markers and interacts with the aspectual character of the situation.

correct.text: We walked from the gate to the bridge.
The clinic stayed open from nine until noon.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Bounding duration supplies the temporal limits of a state or activity. Non-bounding duration measures time associated with an event that already has an endpoint.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.2 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Some predicates support both construals, with completion entailed only on the relevant endpoint reading.

correct.text: They rehearsed for two hours.
They repaired the lift in two hours.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Spend can describe time devoted to an activity, while take can measure the time required to reach an endpoint.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.2 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: With spend, completion can be inferred but can also be explicitly cancelled.

correct.text: We spent a day clearing the yard.
It took us a day to clear the yard.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Bounding duration can give an overall span, a starting point, an endpoint, or both endpoints.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: When only one endpoint is given, the other may be supplied by context or tense.

correct.text: We waited for forty minutes.
We waited from noon until one.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: How long is the usual question for bounding duration. A question about the start or finish can target an individual endpoint.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Questions such as until when are possible but less usual.

correct.text: How long did the crew wait?
When did the crew stop waiting?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A motion clause can accept bounding duration when the motion is construed without a required endpoint.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: A goal that entails arrival can block the simple activity reading.

correct.text: We drove along the coast for an hour.
We walked toward the lighthouse for twenty minutes.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A duration adjunct can measure the state resulting from an event if the predicate and context make that state available.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: An instantaneous event does not automatically license a duration adjunct through an inferred result.

correct.text: I borrowed the drill for three days.
They sent the children outside for an hour.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A bounding duration adjunct can measure a series of events even when an individual event cannot extend through the stated interval.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: A single clause can specify duration at both the individual-event and series levels.

correct.text: The alarm rang every morning for a month.
She gave a ten-minute talk every Friday for a year.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Scope of negation with bounding duration
statement: Negation may deny the stated duration, or the duration may specify how long a negative state continued.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Some sentences allow either scope depending on context.

correct.text: The meeting did not last two hours.
We did not hear from them until Tuesday.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Scope of negation with bounding duration
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Overall duration can be expressed by a bare NP, a for phrase, or an adverb with a duration reading.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Some duration adverbs also have frequency readings.

correct.text: We stayed a week.
The screen went blank briefly.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Since and from can introduce starting points, while until and till can introduce endpoints. The markers differ in their complement options.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: American English through can mark an inclusive final period.

correct.text: We worked from lunch until the lights went out.
I have felt better since leaving the city.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Duration versus location with during, between and since
statement: During and between locate events within an interval and can imply that an event occupied it. Since can introduce either a temporal location or the starting point of duration.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: An implication of continuous duration with during or between can be cancelled.

correct.text: The parcel arrived during lunch.
We have been waiting since noon.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Duration versus location with during, between and since
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: In and within can measure time to an accomplishment or achievement. Future in phrases can also locate an event relative to the present.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.4 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: The in or within construction can suggest a shorter interval than expected. The take construction need not carry that implication.

correct.text: They assembled the stage in an hour.
The doctor arrived within twenty minutes.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Continuation and inception with still and already
statement: Still presents a situation as continuing at the reference time. Already presents it as having begun or been achieved by that time.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §8 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Both can convey expectations about timing, with the details supplied by context.

correct.text: The office is still open.
The office is already open.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Continuation and inception with still and already
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Polarity and questions with still, already and yet
statement: Still can present a negative situation as continuing. Yet commonly appears in negative clauses and questions about whether an expected change has occurred.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §8 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Negation can also take scope over still or already in suitable contexts.

correct.text: The lights still are not working.
Have the lights come on yet?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Polarity and questions with still, already and yet
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Perfect and progressive accumulation with still and already
statement: Already can modify a perfect that reports a completed event. Still can combine with a perfect when the clause describes an ongoing state or a continuing level of progress.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §8 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: A simple completed-event reading generally resists still.

correct.text: She has already read the report.
She has still read only ten pages.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Perfect and progressive accumulation with still and already
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Already can mark an existing amount as significant in an actual or proposed accumulation.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §8 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: The reading can concern a present state without asserting its exact starting time.

correct.text: We already have three printers, and purchasing wants another.
She already has two jobs and is considering a third.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Variety and construction effects with already and yet
statement: Already and yet can occur with perfective preterites in some varieties. Affirmative have yet to expresses that an expected event has not occurred.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §8 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Perfective preterite usage varies across English varieties.

correct.text: Have they replied yet?
We have yet to receive a reply.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Variety and construction effects with already and yet
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Frequency adjuncts quantify occasions or instances of a situation and typically indicate a repeated or distributed situation.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: A single occasion can also be counted, as with once.

correct.text: She visited the archive twice.
The backups usually finish before dawn.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Bounding frequency counts occurrences. Non-bounding frequency describes a rate, tendency or distribution across occasions.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: A clause can combine the two types when they quantify at different levels.

correct.text: She lectured ten times.
She lectured regularly for a semester.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Bounding frequency uses forms such as once, twice and count NPs with time. Non-bounding frequency has adverbial and phrasal realizations.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: An ordinal time phrase can locate an occurrence in a series instead of counting all occurrences.

correct.text: We checked twice.
We check from time to time.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A time expression can quantify recurring occasions or locate a situation at a particular time.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Locative expressions can identify individual occasions inside a frequency construction.

correct.text: We visit every winter.
We visited last winter.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Frequency can quantify occasions on which a negative situation obtains, or negation can deny a stated frequency.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Some placements permit more than one interpretation, depending on the adjunct and focus.

correct.text: She often does not take the bus.
She does not often take the bus.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A quantified NP can determine the set over which a frequency adjunct applies, or frequency can quantify occasions on which an NP statement holds.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Scope depends on the quantifiers, construction and context.

correct.text: Every tenant sometimes uses the courtyard.
Sometimes every tenant uses the courtyard.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Non-bounding frequency quantifies relevant occasions, whose domain can be supplied by a subordinate clause, context or focus.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: The relevant set need not include all times or all possible events.

correct.text: The instructor sometimes gives hints when the problems are difficult.
The caretaker always locks up after evening classes.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Frequency can combine with the progressive. Habitual readings depend on cues that identify repeated situations, and always with the progressive can carry an evaluative implication.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §9 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: The progressive by itself need not describe a habitual situation.

correct.text: She is cycling to work every day this month.
He is always leaving the gate open.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Serial-order adjuncts identify an occurrence by its position in a series. Scope can determine which participants or circumstances are held constant across that series.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §10 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: A contextual alternative can determine what counts as a prior occurrence.

correct.text: Mina performed the piece for the third time.
For the first time, the club met outdoors.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Again can indicate that a whole event recurs or that an earlier state is restored.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §10 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: A restoration reading need not imply a previous instance of the action named by the verb.

correct.text: Mina rang the bell again.
Mina opened the window and later closed it again.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Clause degree can quantify the intensity of a property or situation, emphasize completion, or indicate proximity to an endpoint.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §11 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: A single form can express degree or manner in different contexts.

correct.text: I like the design a lot.
She nearly dropped the tray.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Maximal degree adjuncts can emphasize completion or a very high degree, with individual adverbs favoring particular predicates.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §11 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Quite can also have a moderate reading with a different predicate.

correct.text: She completely removed the stain.
I absolutely reject the proposal.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Multal items express high degree and moderate items express an intermediate degree. Adverbs vary in which predicates they combine with.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §11 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Very generally needs an intervening expression such as much when degree applies to a verb.

correct.text: He deeply regretted the decision.
The plans changed somewhat.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Paucal expressions give a low degree. Minimal items such as at all are often licensed in non-affirmative environments.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §11 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Some inherently negative minimizers differ in distribution from non-affirmative items.

correct.text: The temperature dropped slightly.
If the temperature drops at all, tell me.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Almost and nearly can present a situation as approaching an endpoint or threshold, usually suggesting it did not reach it.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §11 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Approximators differ in the strength of their implications and in lexical distribution.

correct.text: The vase almost fell.
We nearly missed the last train.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Enough and related expressions specify degree relative to a threshold or comparison. A following clause can make the threshold explicit.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §11 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Too requires an appropriate degree-bearing expression when it applies to a verb.

correct.text: We practiced enough to pass.
She valued the time too much to cancel.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Negation can deny a degree while leaving a weaker assertion available. Degree can also modify a negative attitude or preference in suitable contexts.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §11 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Metalinguistic negation can reject a choice of wording or its strength instead of denying the proposition.

correct.text: I do not fully understand the plan.
I very much do not want to move.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Negating maximal degree can leave a high but incomplete degree. Negating a high-degree expression can suggest a low degree.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §11 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Under negation, quite generally has the maximal reading in this construction.

correct.text: I do not quite agree.
They do not meet much.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Under negation, a bit can pattern with minimal at all. Negating an approximator can emphasize the distance from a threshold.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §11 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: A little and slightly are less readily used under ordinary negation.

correct.text: I did not enjoy the show a bit.
We did not nearly finish the inventory.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Cause and result as clause relations
statement: A causal adjunct presents the cause as subordinate to its consequence. A result adjunct presents the consequence as subordinate to its cause.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §12 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Related propositions can also appear in separate clauses linked by context or a connective.

correct.text: The ferry was late because the fog had thickened.
The fog had thickened, so the ferry was late.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Cause and result as clause relations
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A purpose adjunct gives an intended outcome. A reason adjunct gives an explanation that ordinarily commits the speaker to the proposition it expresses.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §12.1 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: A reason clause expressing a desire can also imply a purpose, and a purpose may never be achieved.

correct.text: She left early to catch the ferry.
She left early because the roads were icy.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Temporal relations of purposes and reasons
statement: An intended outcome typically follows the action that serves it, whereas a reason can precede, accompany, or in suitable contexts follow the situation explained.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §12.1 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Future reasons can concern a known or anticipated situation.

correct.text: He packed a snack to eat on the train.
He is nervous because the interview is tomorrow.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Temporal relations of purposes and reasons
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Purpose can be expressed by finite clauses introduced by expressions such as so that or in order that, and by certain for phrases.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §12.2 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: A finite purpose clause commonly contains a modal, but a modal is unnecessary in some contexts.

correct.text: I lowered the blind so that we could see the screen.
We played for fun.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Subject expression in marked purpose infinitivals
statement: An overt subject in a purpose infinitival can be introduced by for, including after in order. Subjectless infinitivals also occur after in order or so as.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §12.2 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: So as does not license the corresponding overt for-subject construction.

correct.text: We opened both doors in order for the crew to enter safely.
She lowered her voice so as to avoid waking the baby.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Subject expression in marked purpose infinitivals
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: The matrix subject typically supplies the understood subject of a purpose infinitival. With a bare purpose infinitival, another participant or an implicit agent can supply it.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §12.2 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: The interpretation can depend on the construction and context.

correct.text: Rae went upstairs to check the fuse.
The manager hired Nia to oversee payroll.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An ungoverned purpose infinitival can contain a gap linked to a matrix NP, including in object position or as the complement of a preposition.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §12.2 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: The infinitival can have its own overt subject even when a non-subject element is missing.

correct.text: I bought them for the children to play with.
She brought a brush to paint the trim with.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An infinitival can modify a noun within an NP or function as a clause-level purpose adjunct. Its position and the resulting interpretation can distinguish the structures.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §12.2 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Some sentence-final infinitivals support both analyses.

correct.text: A spare blanket to use on the journey was donated yesterday.
We opened the blinds to let in more light.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A conditional or temporal construction can suggest an intended outcome. A purpose adjunct can also identify the goal relative to which a requirement applies.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §12.2 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: The purpose suggested by a temporal clause may depend on contextual knowledge beyond the literal time relation.

correct.text: Leave before the rain starts.
We will have to widen the entrance to admit the forklift.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A purpose adjunct can explain a negative situation or fall under negation and be contrasted with another purpose.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §12.2 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Placement and prosody can influence which scope reading is available.

correct.text: To save electricity, we do not run the fans at night.
We did not call to complain. We called to ask for directions.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Reason can be expressed by prepositions with clausal or nominal complements, and can be inferred from some nonfinite adjuncts.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §12.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Individual markers differ in position, complement choice and information structure.

correct.text: We stayed indoors because the smoke was thick.
The event was cancelled owing to heavy rain.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Reason for with a clausal complement has distributional properties associated with coordination, including resistance to fronting.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §12.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Because introduces a wider range of constructions, including ordinary fronted reason adjuncts.

correct.text: I stayed inside, for the pavement was icy.
We turned back, for it was nearly dark.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Scope and focus with reason markers
statement: Because can introduce a focused reason and can fall under negation. Some other reason markers resist those environments.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §12.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Since and as generally do not substitute for because in this cleft.

correct.text: It was because the lock had jammed that we called maintenance.
We did not cancel just because it rained.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Scope and focus with reason markers
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: So and so that can introduce either an intended outcome or an actual consequence. In the result construction, the consequence is presented as obtaining.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §12.4 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Prosody and context can resolve ambiguity when the wording supports either reading.

correct.text: We added a lamp so that visitors could read the map.
The lamp failed, so the map was hard to read.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Result adjuncts occur at the end and resist focus and ordinary narrow-scope negation. Result so does not alternate with in order.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §12.4 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: A modal can occur in a result clause, but a result clause does not require modal qualification.

correct.text: The wind dropped, so that we could finally hear the speaker.
The latch broke, with the result that the door would not close.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Degree so can license a following that clause. An until adjunct can imply a result when it supplies the endpoint of an activity.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §12.4 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: With until, the causal interpretation depends on the relation between the activity and the endpoint.

correct.text: The room was so dark that I missed the step.
She stirred until the sauce thickened.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A concessive adjunct presents its proposition as true and signals that it could ordinarily support an expectation contrary to the matrix situation.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §13.1 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: The strength of the expectation varies with the context and can be weak.

correct.text: Although the trail was steep, the children kept walking.
The cafe stayed open although the street was flooded.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Concession can be expressed by although or though with clausal complements and by despite or in spite of with suitable complements.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §13.2 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Although and though can take reduced clauses, while despite and in spite of allow nominal complements.

correct.text: Though working late, Mina answered the call.
Despite the delay, we caught the train.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A concessive adjunct generally resists direct questioning but can occur inside a contrast under negation.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §13.2 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Availability of contrast depends on the form of the adjunct and construction.

correct.text: We hired her although she was inexperienced.
They hired her not despite her age but because of it.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Whereas and contrastive while can juxtapose situations. But can coordinate contrasting clauses with a meaning related to concessive subordination.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §13.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: A contrast need not imply the kind of expectation associated with a prototypical concession.

correct.text: Mina works upstairs, whereas Dev works downstairs.
The room was small, but it was comfortable.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Even if can concede a possibility while presenting the matrix outcome as holding regardless. Some predicative if constructions have a concessive interpretation.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §13.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Even though normally presents its subordinate proposition as true. Even if can have a factually conceded interpretation in suitable contexts.

correct.text: We will play even if it rains.
The plan is ambitious, if costly.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A conditional construction pairs a protasis giving the condition with an apodosis expressing the associated outcome or proposition.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §14 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: The apodosis need not be a declarative statement, and the protasis can follow it.

correct.text: If the alarm sounds, leave the building.
We will start if the crew arrives.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Open and remote conditionals differ in grammatical form and in the way the speaker presents the condition's status.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §14 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Remoteness is a grammatical distinction and cannot be inferred from an estimate of probability alone.

correct.text: If the gate is locked, we will use the side entrance.
If the gate were locked, we would use the side entrance.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Core relation in an open if conditional
statement: An open if conditional excludes the combination in which the condition holds and the associated proposition fails.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §14.1.1 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: The construction does not itself make the condition necessary for the outcome.

correct.text: If the battery is flat, the motor will not start.
If a whole number is divisible by four, it is even.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Core relation in an open if conditional
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A conditional often suggests that the consequent follows from the condition. It can instead make the consequent relevant to the listener under that condition.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §14.1.1 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: On the relevance reading, the cable can be in the drawer regardless of whether it is needed.

correct.text: If the pipe freezes, it may burst.
If you need a spare cable, there is one in the drawer.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An ordinary if clause can suggest that the outcome depends on the stated condition being met.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §14.1.1 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Context or an explicit continuation can cancel the suggested converse.

correct.text: If the weather improves, we will eat outside.
If the weather improves, we will eat outside, and we might do so even if it does not.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An open condition often suggests uncertainty about whether it holds, but a speaker can use the same construction while committing to its truth or falsity.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §14.1.1 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: The suggestion of uncertainty is an implicature.

correct.text: If Rae is still here, she will be at her desk.
If the bell rings, and it will, use the rear door.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Reversing and negating both parts can preserve the core exclusion while changing the inference about what explains what.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §14.1.1 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Equivalent truth conditions do not guarantee equivalent explanatory or conversational effects.

correct.text: If the lift is moving, its indicator is lit.
If the indicator is not lit, the lift is not moving.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An if clause can restrict the occasions over which a repeated or habitual situation is described.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §14.1.1 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: A frequency adjunct can specify how regularly the outcome holds on relevant occasions.

correct.text: She cycled to work if she started early enough.
We usually eat outside if the weather is mild.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: The time of a condition and the time of its associated proposition can differ. Present tense can refer to future time in an open protasis.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §14.1.2 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Future-oriented will can occur in a protasis in special interpretations, including when a prediction is being entertained.

correct.text: If the crew arrives tomorrow, show them the new entrance.
If the delivery came yesterday, the parcel should be on the shelf now.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Modal and subjunctive choices in open conditionals
statement: An open apodosis can carry different modal qualifications. A plain-form subjunctive protasis is also available in a restricted formal pattern.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §14.1.2 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: The subjunctive pattern is much less usual than indicative alternatives.

correct.text: If it rains, the roads may flood.
If any objection be raised, refer it to the chair.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Modal and subjunctive choices in open conditionals
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An open protasis can license non-affirmative items such as at all or yet, with the choice of expression interacting with expectations.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §14.1.2 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Affirmative alternatives such as already can occur when the context supports the relevant expectation.

correct.text: If you are at all uncertain, call the office.
If the parcel has not arrived yet, contact dispatch.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Only if marks a necessary condition. Whether the condition is also sufficient can depend on the context or be stated explicitly.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §14.1.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: The only-if construction can suggest sufficiency without encoding it.

correct.text: You can enter only if your pass is valid.
The device activates if and only if both switches are on.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Even if presents the outcome as holding in the highlighted case and can suggest that it also holds in relevant alternatives.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §14.1.3 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Focus can make the highlighted case the least expected, or the minimal case sufficient for the outcome.

correct.text: We will sail even if it rains.
You must retake the course even if you fail just one exam.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Remote conditionals often suggest that a present or past condition is false. The inference can remain open when the speaker is uncertain.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §14.2.1 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: A remote past conditional can be used to reason about an unresolved possibility.

correct.text: If the pump were working, the tank would be full.
If she had taken the key, the lock would now be open.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Remote future conditions and tentative requests
statement: Remote forms can present a future condition as unlikely or make an appeal more tentative.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §14.2.1 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Polite use need not indicate that compliance is unlikely.

correct.text: If the flight were cancelled, we would take the train.
I would be grateful if you could check the totals.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Remote future conditions and tentative requests
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: If only can present a condition as desired or as the obstacle to a hoped-for outcome.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §14.2.1 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: The same wording can occur in an independent wish or within a conditional construction.

correct.text: If only we had more time.
We could finish tonight if only the lift were working.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Tense and mood in remote protases
statement: Remote protases can use modal preterite, irrealis were, or a preterite perfect, with time interpreted in context.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §14.2.2 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: The time of the protasis and the time of the apodosis can differ.

correct.text: If she were here now, she would help.
If they had checked yesterday, we would know by now.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Tense and mood in remote protases
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: The canonical remote apodosis uses a modal construction, commonly with would, could, might, or should.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §14.2.2 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: An imperative open apodosis lacks a direct canonical remote counterpart.

correct.text: If the gate were open, we could walk through.
If I knew the answer, I would tell you.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Should and were to can mark special conditional protases. Were to can present a remote future contingency.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §14.2.2 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Should can occur with an open directive apodosis.

correct.text: If you should need assistance, ring the bell.
If the bridge were to close, we would have to turn back.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Certain conditional protases omit if and place had, were, or should before the subject.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §14.2.2 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: The construction is lexically restricted and does not allow general do-support.

correct.text: Had I known, I would have called.
Should you need help, ring the bell.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A perfect in the protasis or modal apodosis can add remoteness even when the situation referred to lies in the future relative to speech time.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §14.2.2 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: The time interpretation depends on the full construction and context, including any explicit time adjunct.

correct.text: If you had told me you were busy, I would have come tomorrow.
If the office had stayed open, I would have picked up the parcel tomorrow.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Modal preterite and ordinary past readings
statement: A preterite in a conditional can express modal remoteness, past time, or backshift. Similar surface forms can therefore support different analyses.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §14.2.2 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Habitual past context and reported speech can produce forms that resemble remote conditionals.

correct.text: If we got home late, the caretaker would lock the gate.
She said that if they arrived late, they would miss dinner.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Modal preterite and ordinary past readings
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Some conditional constructions combine a remote-looking protasis with an apodosis lacking the canonical remote modal pattern.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §14.2.2 of Chapter 8.

exceptions.description: Relevance to the addressee can support the mixed pattern.

statement: In inversion the negative inflected auxiliary precedes the subject, while separate not normally follows it.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §2.1 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: Formal patterns can put separate not before certain subjects, and negative inflection has lexical restrictions.

correct.text: Didn't Mina call?

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Subclausal primary negation under an adjunct
statement: Primary negation can negate a predicate within the scope of a preceding adjunct, while the clause remains syntactically positive.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §2.1 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: The analysis depends on whether the preceding adjunct has scope over the negative predicate.

correct.text: She often isn't at her desk when I call.
They sometimes don't answer the door.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Subclausal primary negation under an adjunct
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Negative imperatives ordinarily use do not or don't, including with be.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §2.2 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: An overt imperative subject can occur, and contracted and uncontracted forms differ in placement.

correct.text: Do not be late.
Don't open the rear door.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Secondary verbal negation uses separate not with infinitival, gerund-participial and past-participial constructions.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §2.3.1 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: Secondary negation has no corresponding negative inflection of a nonfinite lexical verb.

correct.text: They decided not to wait.
Any form not signed by Friday will expire.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Not following a modal can take semantic scope below or above that modal even when it marks primary negation syntactically.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §2.3.2 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: The first normally requires non-opening, while the second removes the requirement to open.

correct.text: They must not open the gate.
They need not open the gate.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Secondary negation after a positive modal
statement: In a restricted construction, a separate not following a positive modal can belong to its nonfinite complement.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §2.3.2 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: The secondary reading is relatively rare and can require explicit contextual or prosodic support.

correct.text: You can not reply if you prefer to stay silent.
You may not reply if you would rather leave it unanswered.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Secondary negation after a positive modal
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A negative auxiliary can coexist with separate not marking secondary negation. The matrix clause remains syntactically negative.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §2.3.2 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: The semantic effect depends on whether the negatives are adjacent in scope or separated by a modal.

correct.text: You can't not tell her.
I didn't not listen.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Infinitival to separating an auxiliary from not
statement: When infinitival to precedes not, it separates the negator from the higher auxiliary and locates it in the infinitival construction.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §2.3.2 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: With not before to, attachment can depend on the surrounding construction.

correct.text: Their aim is to not change the process.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Infinitival to separating an auxiliary from not
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Adjuncts separating a negator from an auxiliary
statement: An intervening adjunct can make it clear that not belongs to the nonfinite complement of an auxiliary.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §2.3.2 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: Without the adjunct, context or prosody may be needed to distinguish primary and secondary negation.

correct.text: You can simply not reply.
