burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Adjuncts separating a negator from an auxiliary
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Negative requests with an inverted auxiliary
statement: A question-shaped request can use not to negate the requested action in the nonfinite complement.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §2.3.2 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: An inverted question without please can also have an interpretation with matrix negation.

correct.text: Would you please not lean on the glass?
Could you please not move the papers?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Negative requests with an inverted auxiliary
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Not can combine with an initial quantifier to deny the amount or proportion expressed by the quantifier.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.1 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: The position of the quantified phrase and the relevant polarity test matter when assessing the containing clause.

correct.text: Not all of the lamps worked.
Not every visitor had a ticket.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Not one can deny that even a single member meets the condition. Not with a higher numeral can indicate that a measure falls below that numeral.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.1 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: The higher-numeral pattern has a restricted distribution and does not behave like the negative quantifier not one.

correct.text: Not one driver stopped.
Not three months ago, the bridge was open.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Litotic not a little and not a few
statement: Not a little and not a few can convey a substantial amount or number through litotes.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.1 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: These combinations need not make the clause syntactically negative.

correct.text: The announcement caused not a little confusion.
Not a few volunteers stayed behind to help.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Litotic not a little and not a few
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Not even rejects a focused case, often one at the low end of an expectation scale. Not only adds another case beyond an accepted one.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.1 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: Fronted not only can trigger inversion even when the corresponding proposition is affirmed.

correct.text: Not even our captain knew the route.
Not only did our captain know the route, but she also knew the currents.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Not can negate an adjective phrase with a modifier such as very or quite.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.1 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: Direct negation of a bare adjective is more restricted in these environments.

correct.text: We had a not very productive meeting.
The connection seemed not entirely secure.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Not can modify an affixally negative adjective and convey a qualified assessment.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.1 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: The two negative expressions need not yield the same interpretation as the unprefixed positive adjective.

correct.text: The design is not unattractive.
The payment is not insignificant.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Not can modify some adverbs without making the containing clause negative.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.1 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: The pattern is lexically restricted. The clause can independently carry verbal negation.

correct.text: Not surprisingly, the queue grew.
Not unreasonably, she asked for a receipt.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Clausal and subclausal not with PPs
statement: Not with a fronted PP can mark clausal negation or deny only the value expressed by the PP.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.1 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: Inversion and the entailments of the clause help distinguish the readings.

correct.text: Not at any point did the alarm sound.
Not for the first time, the alarm sounded late.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Clausal and subclausal not with PPs
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Not can negate a verbless supplement while the main clause retains its own polarity.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.1 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: The relation between the supplement and the main situation can be inferred from context.

correct.text: Not an experienced climber, Mina took the easier route.
Not fully awake, Dev reached for the wrong switch.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A detached not that clause can reject an inference that the preceding utterance might otherwise invite.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.1 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: The supplement has its own negative content and need not change the preceding clause's polarity.

correct.text: I will cover the shift. Not that I am eager to do it.
She kept the letter. Not that she agreed with it.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Not can mark an alternative rejected in a coordination or a detached contrast.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.1 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: The negation can be restricted to a coordinate while the larger clause remains positive.

correct.text: We are leaving not on Friday but on Saturday.
Bring a pencil, not a pen.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An independent final not can retract or reverse an apparently positive utterance for rhetorical effect.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.1 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: This construction is informal and differs prosodically from ordinary integrated negation.

correct.text: That was a brilliant idea, not!
I am thrilled to be working late again, not!

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: No, none, nobody and related forms can mark absolute clausal negation without a negative verb.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.2.1 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: The effect depends on the constituent's position and interpretation.

correct.text: Nobody answered, did they?
Mina had received nothing, and neither had Dev.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Alternation with verbal negation and any
statement: A clause with an absolute non-verbal negator often has a counterpart with verbal negation and a corresponding any form.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.2.1 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: The alternation is not generally available when the negative expression is in subject position.

correct.text: We found nothing.
We did not find anything.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Alternation with verbal negation and any
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Predicative no can have a verbal-negation counterpart in some constructions. The distance between verb and negative constituent can limit alternation.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.2.1 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: Idiomatic or evaluative predicative expressions can lack a natural counterpart, and a distant replacement can change the scope.

correct.text: This is no place for a picnic.
This is not any place for a picnic.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A non-verbal negator inside a subordinate construction ordinarily has a local interpretation. Some constructions allow it to affect the interpretation of the matrix clause.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.2.1 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: Polarity tests and the relation between the clauses can help determine whether a wider analysis is available.

correct.text: She said that nobody had called.
They promised to make no changes.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A negative NP in a PP, an evaluative expression, or an NP with an implicit predication can leave the containing clause positive.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.2.2 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: A phrase with a compressed predication can admit a different scope analysis in context.

correct.text: We managed with no spare parts.
That was no small achievement, wasn't it?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Approximate negators include the determinatives few and little, frequency adverbs rarely and seldom, and degree adverbs barely, hardly and scarcely.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.3 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: Comparative and superlative forms of few and little do not behave like their plain forms in the polarity tests.

correct.text: Few students applied.
The needle barely moved.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Approximate negation often suggests a small nonzero quantity or frequency, unlike absolute negation.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.3 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: The inference of a nonzero value can be cancelled in appropriate contexts.

correct.text: Few tickets were sold.
She rarely misses a rehearsal.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Few presents the quantity as low and can act as a negator. A few presents a positive quantity and behaves differently in polarity tests.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.3 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: A few can be followed by a correction to a larger quantity without adopting the polarity of few.

correct.text: Few of the lights worked.
A few of the lights worked.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Hardly can occur with a past perfect and a following when clause to indicate that one event followed the other very closely.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.3 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: The construction conveys close succession rather than denying that the first event occurred.

correct.text: I had hardly sat down when the phone rang.
She had hardly closed the door when the dog barked.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Downward entailment as a semantic diagnostic
statement: In a downward-entailing environment, replacing a class with a relevant subclass can preserve entailment.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.3 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: The comparison requires a stable contextual standard and reference class.

correct.text: Few visitors bought a souvenir.
Few visitors bought a ceramic souvenir.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Downward entailment as a semantic diagnostic
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Rarely and seldom can support downward entailments when the compared situations are assessed against the same reference class.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.3 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: A change in the comparison class can invalidate the apparent inference.

correct.text: She rarely reads fiction.
She rarely reads historical fiction.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Approximate negators can pass tests for clausal negation, including reversed tags and negative additive continuations.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.3 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: Late or embedded placement can favor subclausal negation, and the approximate negators differ in behavior.

correct.text: Few members spoke, did they?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An approximate negator can remain within a smaller constituent while the clause has positive polarity.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.3 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: A clause containing a restricted negative expression can still license a positive-polarity continuation.

correct.text: We could manage with barely any supplies.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Affixal versus verbal negation on a scale
statement: A negative prefix can reverse a scale or select its negative region, while verbal negation denies a predication.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.4 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: On a gradable scale, intermediate cases can satisfy neither of the two contrasting adjective predicates.

correct.text: The error is not common.
The error is uncommon.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Affixal versus verbal negation on a scale
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Degree modification of a negatively prefixed adjective measures the negative property. Negation of a degree-modified positive adjective denies that degree.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §3.4 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: The contrast is especially visible with gradable adjectives and need not apply the same way to complementary predicates.

correct.text: The result is not very common.
The result is very uncommon.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Polarity-sensitive expressions favor either negative or positive environments, depending on the expression and its meaning.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: The orientation describes distribution and does not by itself make the clause negative or positive.

correct.text: We do not need it any longer.
We already have a replacement.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A positive clause can be non-affirmative for polarity licensing, as in questions and certain subordinate constructions.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: Different non-affirmative environments license different sets of expressions.

correct.text: Do you need it any longer?
Have you ever seen this before?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Negatively oriented expressions include some uses of any and yet, certain auxiliary uses, and idiomatic minimizers.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.1 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: The restrictions apply to particular senses or constructions, and a literal reading can have a different distribution.

correct.text: She has not called yet.
They did not lift a finger to help.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Until can freely specify the endpoint of an ongoing situation. With punctual or telic predicates it can occur in a negative construction that denies occurrence before a boundary.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.1 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: Polarity sensitivity depends on the aspectual construction, rather than a general restriction on until.

correct.text: We will stay until dusk.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Negative polarity items versus negative idioms
statement: An NPI can occur with negation that independently marks its clause. A negative idiom can require a particular negator as part of its conventional wording.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.1.1 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: Tests that vary the position or form of negation can help distinguish a freely licensed item from an idiom.

correct.text: They did not stay for long.
The soup was not half bad.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Negative polarity items versus negative idioms
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Strength and register of negative orientation
statement: Some NPIs are strongly restricted to negative contexts. Others have a wider distribution, and an apparently identical form can have a register-specific affirmative use.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.1.2 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: The second much belongs to a different construction and does not establish the same distribution for ordinary clause-final much.

correct.text: I do not enjoy sailing much.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Strength and register of negative orientation
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Some NPIs occur in neutral questions, while strongly oriented idioms can require an interpretation closer to negation.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.1.2 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: A question can admit a strong item when it conveys a negative expectation or challenges an assumption.

correct.text: Did anyone call?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Some uses of some, already and other expressions favor affirmative environments and resist the scope of ordinary negation.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.2 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: The restriction applies to the intended sense, and negative clauses can accommodate these forms when scope or context supports them.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: PPIs outside the scope of negation
statement: A positive-polarity expression can occur in a sentence containing negation when the expression takes wider scope.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.2 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: The negative's presence alone does not determine whether it has scope over the polarity item.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: PPIs outside the scope of negation
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Metalinguistic correction, echoed denial, and certain layered negative contexts can admit expressions that resist ordinary negation.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.2 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: These uses rely on discourse or scope and do not generalize to all negative sentences.

correct.text: It is not pretty large. It is enormous.

statement: Many PPIs occur in questions, including biased negative questions that invite a positive answer.

statement: An affirmative existential with some can correspond to verbal negation with any or to non-verbal negation with no.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Some and any in polar questions

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Some and any in polar questions
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

statement: Positive and negative clauses can express parallel continuation or additive meanings with different polarity-sensitive forms.

concept: Overt negators and interrogatives as licensers
statement: An NPI can occur in the scope of a negator or in certain interrogatives without overt negation.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Overt negators and interrogatives as licensers
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Polarity in why and why-not infinitivals
statement: A why infinitival can question the point of an action and admit an NPI. The corresponding why not construction often presents an affirmative suggestion.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.4 of Chapter 9.

exceptions.description: The pragmatic function can matter more for licensing than the overt presence of not.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Polarity in why and why-not infinitivals
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Covertly negative predicates and their complements
statement: Predicates such as fail, prevent, deny and doubt can license NPIs in suitable clausal or clause-like complements.

exceptions.description: Licensing is sensitive to the lexical meaning and to which constituent falls within its scope.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Covertly negative predicates and their complements
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Some evaluative and emotive predicates can admit NPIs in their complements, even where the embedded situation is understood to have occurred.

statement: Certain downward-entailing quantified subjects can license NPIs in the predicate.

concept: Bare relatives with subject versus embedded subject gaps

statement: Relative who normally takes a personal antecedent, while which normally takes a nonpersonal antecedent.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

statement: An integrated relative is part of a nominal constituent. A supplementary relative is set apart prosodically and typically by punctuation in writing.

concept: Multiple gaps and exceptional final gapping

concept: Pronoun case in a gapped coordinate
statement: A pronoun subject without an overt finite verb in a gapped clause may appear in nominative or accusative case, subject to stylistic and structural preferences.

exceptions.description: Where both subject and object are pronouns, the accusative subject is less acceptable; a gapped subject with nominative is more formal.

concept: Basic coordination requires equivalent syntactic functions
statement: Outside special joint, lexicalised, rhetorical or minor motivated patterns, two bare coordinates must each stand in the same syntactic relation to the surrounding material.
condition: When two dependents share one governor in ordinary basic coordination, each must fulfil the same grammatical function under the relevant sense of that governor.
violation: In an ordinary standard-English basic coordination requires equivalent syntactic functions construction, the coordinates violate the stated syntactic licensing condition.

exceptions.description: Do not apply this error universally to mixed-category expressions with the same function, joint coordinations, syllepsis or special fixed patterns.

correct.text: The visitor arrived yesterday and after lunch.
The actor admired and praised the leader.

incorrect.text: The visitor arrived yesterday and the station.
The actor became and praised the leader.

concept: Infinitival and gerund-participial clause coordination restriction
statement: A subject coordination cannot ordinarily mix an infinitival clause and a gerund-participial clause as bare coordinates, although either category can individually serve as subject.
condition: A single coordination of nonfinite clauses occupying the subject position must not conjoin a to-infinitival with a gerund-participial bare coordinate.
violation: In an ordinary standard-English infinitival and gerund-participial clause coordination restriction construction, the coordinates violate the stated syntactic licensing condition.

exceptions.description: The broader rule of function sameness does permit many unlike-category coordinations, but this particular category pairing is barred.

concept: Singular-noun coordination cannot satisfy a plural determinative
statement: A word-level coordination of singular count nouns remains syntactically singular, so it cannot satisfy a demonstrative or cardinal determiner that selects a plural nominal head.
condition: When a plural demonstrative or numeral selecting a plural nominal directly governs a coordination of two singular nouns used together as the nominal head.
violation: In an ordinary standard-English singular-noun coordination cannot satisfy a plural determinative construction, the coordinates violate the stated syntactic licensing condition.

exceptions.description: Closely associated nouns may form a singular-headed unit with a singular determiner; coordination at full NP level has different number behavior. Semantic anomaly of pairing unrelated nouns is not itself this syntactic violation.

correct.text: I packed this cup and saucer.
She photographed two plates and bowls.

incorrect.text: I packed these cup and saucer.
She photographed two plate and bowl.

concept: Person agreement is stricter than descriptive gender agreement

concept: Reflexive anaphor requires the appropriate local antecedent in a chain
statement: A reflexive anaphor in an embedded clause cannot skip a mismatched local subject to take a more distant nominal as its antecedent.
condition: For a reflexive serving as object of a finite predicate, its person/number/gender must be compatible with a locally licensed subject antecedent, even when that subject is itself anticipatorily anaphoric.
violation: A reflexive is assigned an intended antecedent across a clause boundary although a mismatched local subject blocks that relation.

exceptions.description: A chain can link the reflexive indirectly through a compatible local personal pronoun; this is not a direct long-distance reflexive link.

If she blames herself, Mira will apologize.

concept: Pride lexically requires the subject-bound reflexive object

statement: A comparative inside a content clause can compare two terms within the reported attitude, or compare the reported degree with a degree outside it.
condition: Context guides scope. The wide reading in the cited pattern resists reducing the comparative clause to a bare pronoun.

correct.text: Lee thinks Jo is taller than she is. [possible comparison within Lee's belief]
Lee thinks Jo is taller than she actually is. [comparison with Jo's actual height]

concept: Predicative and attributive comparative phrase scope
statement: A predicative comparative AdjP can supply the counterpart directly. An attributive comparative AdjP can extend the comparative feature to its containing NP, requiring a suitable NP counterpart.
condition: The choice can change the interpretation and acceptability of the same secondary clause.

correct.text: Her truck was heavier than my car had been.
She bought a heavier truck than I had owned.

statement: The comparative feature of an AdvP can remain in that phrase or extend to a larger AdjP or NP.
condition: A degree comparison embedded in a description can require recovery of the containing phrase rather than only the manner adverb.

correct.text: She argued more clearly than I did.
This is a more carefully edited report than we had expected to receive.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

statement: A postpositive comparative AdjP normally retains its own comparative scope, unlike the cited attributive counterpart. Its complement ordinarily cannot be postposed out of it.
condition: Attested examples with wider scope exist, but the extension is not freely available.

correct.text: She bought a van more powerful than her old car had been.
Anyone less patient than Jo would have left.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

concept: NP and PP boundaries in comparative scope
statement: A comparative NP within a PP does not generally pass the comparative feature to the containing PP. Some constructions instead compare the whole PP.
condition: Under NP scope, a preposition needed by the secondary predicate remains overt unless a separate stranding reduction removes more material.

correct.text: She worked on more projects than I had worked on.
She left in a better mood than she had arrived.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: NP and PP boundaries in comparative scope

concept: Exceptional upward scope from comparative adjectives
statement: Some attested comparisons recover an NP counterpart from a matrix comparative adjective that is postpositive or predicative.
condition: The source questions how systematic some cases are and rejects unrestricted extension.

correct.text: They accepted risks greater than we would have accepted.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

statement: A metalinguistic comparison compares the applicability of descriptions, rather than degrees on a single lexical scale.
condition: The core construction uses analytic marking and can compare non-gradable adjectives, NPs and PPs. The cited construction excludes comparative clauses and direct comparison of verbs.

correct.text: The label was more green than blue.
It was more a warning than a promise.
She spoke more out of concern than out of anger.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

statement: Rather than and not so much X as Y can present a contrast in how something is best described.
condition: Both patterns also have ordinary non-metalinguistic uses, depending on context.

correct.text: It was an inconvenience rather than a disaster.
He was not so much angry as embarrassed.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

statement: Analytic degree more expresses superiority where the separate marker is available. Other lexemes prefer or require an inflectional comparative, and some permit both.
condition: The metalinguistic construction can license analytic more with adjectives that ordinarily inflect.

correct.text: This beam is shorter than that one.
This fabric is more durable than that one.
This form is simpler or more simple, depending on the intended phrasing.

concept: Inflectional more and most of much and many
statement: Determinative more is the irregular comparative of much and many; most is the corresponding superlative. Analytic adverb more has a different function.
condition: Plain much readily occurs in non-affirmative contexts. The noun-quantifying more can apply to mass and plural-count nominals.

correct.text: Did the repair cause much trouble? Did it cause more trouble this time?

statement: Analytic less expresses scalar inferiority with a separate marker, including with adjectives that use an inflectional superiority form.
condition: The source distinguishes analytic less from inflectional less, which it develops on the following page.

correct.text: This beam is less long than the other one.
The new coating is less porous than the old one.

statement: Inflectional less can be the comparative of determinative little. Analytic less before an adjective is a different construction and does not alternate with plain little.
condition: Adjective little meaning small is distinct; its inflections littler and littlest are uncommon.

correct.text: We have less water than we need.
This cover is less rigid than the other one.

statement: Much and little orient the quantity scale in opposite directions. More and inflectional less both mark superiority on their own oriented scales.
condition: This differs from analytic less, which marks inferiority on the scale supplied by its head. Much and little do not themselves take analytic less to form a corresponding paradigm.

correct.text: We collected more rainwater than last year.
We collected less rainwater than last year.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

concept: Reverse comparisons with more and less
statement: With opposite-oriented determinatives, X has more than Y and Y has less than X entail one another. Equality comparisons with much and little can convey different background quantities.
condition: Much is the more neutral choice in ordinary quantity questions; little can suggest a low quantity already accepted in context.

correct.text: We have more fuel than they do. They have less fuel than we do.
How much fuel remains?
We have as little fuel as they do.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Reverse comparisons with more and less
burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

statement: Reversing the arguments and changing to an opposite adjective can preserve meaning, produce a one-way entailment, or change the suggested range of both terms.
condition: The source contrasts age, evaluation and temperature. These patterns depend on lexical meaning and context.

correct.text: Jo is older than Lee, and Lee is younger than Jo.
This tool is better than the old one, though both work well.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

statement: Analytic inferiority competes with negated scalar equality and reversed superiority. A superiority paraphrase may lose the background suggestion that an adjective applies to both terms.

correct.text: The first route is less difficult than the second.

The second route is harder than the first.

statement: Adjectival less can contrast with greater without being the comparative of a single plain adjective. It is mainly predicative, with limited attributive uses.
condition: Lesser adds a comparative suffix to an irregular comparative base and is attributive. This established form does not license obsolete double comparatives generally.

correct.text: The actual cost was less than the estimate.
The change affected each team to a greater or lesser extent.
We accepted the lesser risk.

concept: Count and non-count degree determinative paradigms
statement: Much and little quantify non-count nominals; many and few quantify plural count nominals. More serves both quantity types, while negative-oriented comparison has less or fewer according to construction.
condition: Do not infer an identical distribution for all uses of less and fewer.

correct.text: We used as much paper as they did.
We submitted as many forms as they did.
We used fewer sheets this time.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

statement: Ordinary non-count singular quantity uses less rather than fewer.
condition: Plural count nominals can take fewer, while numeral measures of duration, money, age or speed commonly use less.
violation: Fewer quantifies an ordinary singular non-count nominal.

exceptions.description: Plural count nominals can take fewer, while numeral measures of duration, money, age or speed commonly use less.

correct.text: We need less equipment than they do.
The recipe uses less flour than mine.
We need fewer tools than they do.
She arrived less than ten minutes ago.

incorrect.text: We need fewer equipment than they do.
The recipe uses fewer flour than mine.

diagnostic.error_pattern: Fewer quantifies an ordinary singular non-count nominal.
minimal_pairs: We need fewer equipment than they do. ||| We need less equipment than they do.
The recipe uses fewer flour than mine. ||| The recipe uses less flour than mine.
diagnostic.learner_explanation: Ordinary non-count singular quantity uses less rather than fewer. Use less with the non-count nominal.
diagnostic.corrected_paragraph_template: Use less with the non-count nominal.
false_positive_guards: We need fewer tools than they do.
She arrived less than ten minutes ago.

concept: Less with measures, thresholds and plural counts
statement: Less is usual with a numerical amount and in patterns such as a numeral plus or less. Less and fewer can both occur with some thresholds and plural counts.
condition: Fewer is often preferred directly before a plural count noun in formal style. A non-count plural such as pains differs from a count plural.

correct.text: We paid less than twenty dollars.
Fewer than half the voters turned up.
Ten items or less qualifies.

concept: More and less grading singular heads and verbs
statement: More of a and less of a can grade the applicability of a singular count nominal in a predicative NP. Comparative more and less can also modify a verb as degree adjuncts.
condition: Plain much and little are available in equality comparisons, with further restrictions on unmodified verb adjuncts.

correct.text: It was less of a setback than we feared.
The injection hurt less than I expected.
It hurt as much as last time.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: More and less grading singular heads and verbs

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

concept: Would rather with bare infinitival and finite complements
statement: Would rather can take a bare infinitival or a finite complement. The comparison can contrast entire complements or smaller corresponding parts.
condition: Would sooner is an alternative, and would as soon supplies a related equality pattern.

correct.text: I'd rather walk than take the bus.
I'd rather she came on Friday than on Saturday.

statement: Preferential rather than with a bare infinitival requires the adjacent than complement. Contrastive rather than can behave like a coordinator meaning instead of.
condition: In the contrastive construction, a bare infinitival counterpart pairs with another bare infinitival.

correct.text: Rather than wait in the rain, let's go inside.
The machine would restart rather than shut down.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

concept: Pleonastic rather in an expanded comparative complement
statement: Rather than can sometimes reinforce an earlier comparison whose governor is separated from the than phrase.
condition: It is unavailable as a general replacement for than in a simple comparison or with determinative more in the cited pattern.

correct.text: It would be easier to work with a partner, rather than with strangers.

statement: Prefer commonly contrasts an object NP with a to phrase. Infinitival preference normally uses rather than for an overt secondary term.

concept: To complements of superior and inferior
statement: Comparative superior and inferior select to for the secondary term in the cited construction.
condition: They also accept degree modifiers and can have plain evaluative readings with very. A recursive comparison with these adjectives is distinct from double-marking an inflectional comparative.
violation: Than introduces the secondary term of comparative superior or inferior.

concept: Related Latin-derived adjectives and senior genitives

concept: Scalar equality with as and restricted so and such

condition: Non-scalar such and intensifying such without a comparative as phrase have different licensing.

concept: Degree modifiers of scalar equality and inequality
statement: Equality and inequality admit different sets of degree modifiers with some overlap. Much and far modify inequality; nearly and twice are typical with equality.
condition: Very can modify much in very much bigger, but does not directly replace much before the comparative form.

correct.text: The new bag is far lighter.
The new bag is nearly as light as mine.

statement: Multipliers and fractions interact differently with equality and inequality. A third as much gives a fraction of the baseline; a third more adds that fraction to the baseline.
condition: The source records a multiplier reading of four times more that matches four times as much. The equality phrasing makes the intended ratio explicit.

correct.text: The new pump uses a third as much power.
The new pump uses a third more power.
The new pump uses twice as much power.

statement: The can modify a comparative expression in several constructions, including correlatives and the more or the less patterns.

statement: Comparative the can modify a comparative in an adjective, adverb, verbal or determinative construction. Its omissibility depends on the construction.
condition: It is retained in all the more, the cited supplement, and fronted purpose the better. In this noncorrelative term construction it is unavailable with an overt or anaphorically recovered secondary term. Set comparison can independently license the better.

concept: No sooner and overlapping temporal idioms

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

condition: Regarding uses can omit be concerned in some varieties. Go so far as to marks an extreme action, and insofar as marks extent.

correct.text: I'll stay so long as the door remains open.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

concept: Comparative and additive uses of as well

condition: With possibility modals, might as well can express a grudging suggestion or dissatisfaction. Just as well can express that something was fortunate.

statement: Know better than to conveys awareness that an action is inappropriate. In the cited as best construction, best occurs with can.

statement: In the basic correlative construction, the subordinate adjunct follows the main clause. In the common fronted version, it comes first and the main comparative phrase is also fronted.

statement: Correlative comparatives express parallel changes on two scales. Reversing which clause is subordinate can change the claim.

statement: The correlative adjunct is a subordinate content clause even though its comparative fronting does not uniquely mark subordination.

concept: Present tense and modal remoteness after as if
statement: With a present matrix, present tense in the complement can present an appearance as an open possibility. Irrealis were or a modal preterite can mark remoteness.
condition: Irrealis can convey counterfactuality. A modal preterite can also convey weaker commitment without entailing falsity.

correct.text: She talks as if she knows the answer.
She talks as though she knew the answer.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Present tense and modal remoteness after as if
burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

concept: Irrealis and backshift with past matrix as if
statement: After a past matrix, irrealis were can express modal remoteness or occur as an extended formal usage without a counterfactual implication.
condition: Was can be a less formal variant in remote contexts. A preterite perfect can mark backshift or past time in relevant remote readings but is less usual there than were or a simple preterite. Extended were can occasionally occur with a present matrix.

correct.text: They treated the intern as though she were the owner.
He stared at the empty bench as though he were remembering someone.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

concept: Infinitival and verbless as if complements
statement: Compound as if and as though accept subjectless infinitival and verbless complements.
condition: The infinitival generally suggests apparent purpose, typically with an agent or personification. The verbless pattern can correspond to omission of subject and be.

correct.text: Lee leaned closer as if to read the engraving.
The balloon hung in the air as though weightless.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Infinitival and verbless as if complements
burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

concept: Scalar as followed by a conditional if phrase
statement: In scalar as … as if, the second as heads the comparative phrase and takes a conditional if phrase as complement.
condition: Occasional though in this scalar construction is analyzed as a blend and has questionable acceptability. The non-scalar as though compound has its own regular uses.

correct.text: The room was as cold as if the windows had been open all night.
She moved as quietly as if the baby were asleep.

concept: Like with NP for resemblance and as for capacity
statement: Non-scalar term comparisons of resemblance use like with a noun phrase. Capacity as with a noun phrase expresses the role in which someone acts.
condition: Like a supervisor leaves open whether the person is one. As a supervisor identifies the capacity in which they act.
violation: As is used with a bare NP to express resemblance in the ordinary non-scalar term comparison.

exceptions.description: As with an NP is valid in the capacity construction. Comparative as can also take a clause.

correct.text: Nina is like her aunt in temperament.
Like Lena, I prefer the earlier train.
I signed the form as the project manager.
As our neighbors do, we support the proposal.

incorrect.text: Nina is as her aunt in temperament.
As Lena, I prefer the earlier train.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Like with NP for resemblance and as for capacity
burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

diagnostic.error_pattern: As is used with a bare NP to express resemblance in the ordinary non-scalar term comparison.

As Lena, I prefer the earlier train. ||| Like Lena, I prefer the earlier train.
diagnostic.learner_explanation: Non-scalar term comparisons of resemblance use like with a noun phrase. Capacity as with a noun phrase expresses the role in which someone acts. Use like with a noun phrase when the phrase expresses resemblance.
diagnostic.corrected_paragraph_template: Use like with a noun phrase when the phrase expresses resemblance.
false_positive_guards: I signed the form as the project manager.

concept: Predicative like phrases with NP complements
statement: Like phrases can function as predicative complements after be and appearance or sense verbs, and in some complex-transitive patterns.
condition: The phrase can mark resemblance or characteristic conduct. Like this also occurs as a predicative adjunct. Feel like a rest expresses desire, and looks like a named individual can express probable identification.

correct.text: The new finish feels like velvet.
The costume made her look more like her aunt.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

statement: Like with an NP can fill a selected manner complement position. With some verbs either of two participants can supply the primary term.
condition: An NP complement stays an NP despite ambiguity. Demonstrative like that can directly specify a manner.

correct.text: Nora treated Leo like the other apprentices.
Please don't handle the samples like that.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

concept: Likeness of predication with like and unlike
statement: A like adjunct can attribute the matrix predicate to the secondary term as backgrounded information. In this reading unlike negates the backgrounded predication.
condition: The matrix subject normally gives the primary term. Integrated manner like does not freely alternate with unlike, while supplementary placement can support the predication reading.

correct.text: Like her neighbor, Jo grows tomatoes.
Unlike her neighbor, Jo grows tomatoes.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Likeness of predication with like and unlike
burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

statement: A fronted like adjunct normally lies outside clausal negation. Medial and final placement can allow either scope, with prosodic detachment favoring wide scope.
condition: A like phrase compares the predication applied to two participants.

correct.text: Like his sister, Arun hadn't heard the announcement.
Arun hadn't heard the announcement, like his sister.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

concept: Personal pronoun case after comparative like
statement: Accusative is standard for a personal pronoun serving as the bare NP complement in the predication adjunct. Clause-initial and post-VP positions require it in this construction.
condition: The pronoun is the entire complement of like in a clause-initial or post-VP adjunct.
violation: The form does not satisfy the requirements of this bare pronoun complement.

exceptions.description: Occasional medial nominatives are attested and analyzed as likely hypercorrections. A pronoun subject of a finite clause after like is a different construction.

correct.text: Like them, Ruth commutes by train.
Ruth commutes by train, like us.
Like we do, Ruth commutes by train.
Ruth, like us, commutes by train.

incorrect.text: Like they, Ruth commutes by train.
Ruth commutes by train, like we.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Personal pronoun case after comparative like
burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

diagnostic.error_pattern: The form does not satisfy the requirements of this bare pronoun complement.
minimal_pairs: Like they, Ruth commutes by train. ||| Like them, Ruth commutes by train.
Ruth commutes by train, like we. ||| Ruth commutes by train, like us.
diagnostic.learner_explanation: Use the object form for a bare personal pronoun after comparative like in this position.
diagnostic.corrected_paragraph_template: Use the object form for a bare personal pronoun after comparative like in this position.
false_positive_guards: Like we do, Ruth commutes by train.
Ruth, like us, commutes by train.

concept: Non-subject primary terms with predication like
statement: The subject usually supplies the primary term. A possessor, embedded complement, locative, or understood entity can supply it in attested examples, which careful prose often reformulates.
condition: The intended comparison is between entities identified by the discourse.

correct.text: Like the old library, the new library has narrow aisles.
As with the old library, the aisles are narrow.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

statement: An integrated manner adjunct under negation denies similarity of manner, often suggesting that the activity still occurs. A demonstrative can specify the manner, and the primary term need not be the subject.
condition: The like phrase is integrated into the VP or directly supplies a manner.

correct.text: These wheels don't turn like the older ones.
Fold the paper like this.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

statement: Some like adjuncts compare a participant or its appearance during an event without attributing the same action to the secondary term. Others evaluate conduct as characteristic of a type of person.
condition: The resemblance is evaluated in the circumstances described by the matrix.

correct.text: The beam spread through the fog like a fan.
I agreed without checking, like a fool.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

statement: Like can modify a nominal or supplement an NP. It can express resemblance, exemplification, or likeness that includes identity; exemplifying like is not confined to informal style.
condition: The like phrase is attached within the nominal or to an NP anchor.

exceptions.description: An apparent comparison between mismatched entities can be stylistically doubtful; a nominal substitute such as that of can clarify the intended comparison.

correct.text: We ordered a lamp like this.
The shop sells unusual spices, like dried lime.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

statement: Like can head a phrase containing a finite comparative clause with a missing predicative, manner, or complement element. It competes with as and, in nominal examples, such as.
condition: A missing element can be understood from the construction and context.

correct.text: You organize files like I do.
She brought a folding stool like you see at campsites.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

statement: Like also licenses a structurally complete finite content clause in patterns comparable to as if or as though. Both finite-clause uses are established, more widely distributed in American English and especially informal in British English.
condition: The finite clause expresses an appearance or hypothetical situation.

correct.text: It looks like the floor is wet.
She guarded the bag like it held her savings.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

statement: Like can precede a PP or a time NP functioning like an adjunct. A reduced-clause analysis is possible, and formal style generally favors as with the corresponding PP.
condition: The complement expresses a location or time of a comparable situation.

correct.text: The roads freeze early here, like in the mountains.
We're closing in August, like last year.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

concept: NP plus PP ambiguity after like
statement: A sequence after like can be a single NP with a nominal PP modifier or a verbless clause with a separate PP. Whether the noun independently licenses the PP and whether it contributes to the comparison help distinguish them.
condition: The PP either restricts the NP referent or contributes a separate element to the comparison.

correct.text: He looks like a student in my class.
She rushed toward the porch like a moth toward a lamp.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: NP plus PP ambiguity after like
burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

statement: Like can take gerund-participial complements. An overt NP followed by an -ing clause can allow NP-modifier and nonfinite-clause analyses. Look like with a gerund-participial can express an apparent future outcome.
condition: The -ing form may head a complement or modify a noun inside it.

correct.text: Solving this puzzle is like sorting beads by touch.
The rain looks like continuing through the night.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

statement: Nothing like can modify a participle, anything like can modify a scalar as phrase, and something like can approximate a number. The like sequence in an ordinary nothing-headed NP has a different structure.
condition: The containing phrase has a participial, adjectival, scalar, or numeral head.

correct.text: We've nothing like finished.
There were something like forty names on the list.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

statement: Nominal like occurs with of or with an anaphorically understood term. Attributive adjectival like can express a similar quantity or type. The likes of is an informal plural pattern.
condition: The secondary term can be expressed with of or recovered from discourse.

correct.text: I'd never seen the like of that display.
The second project received a like amount.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

concept: Like and alike in set comparison
statement: Attributive adjectival like can express likeness within a set. Alike serves as a predicative adjective, manner adverb, or distributive adjunct associated with coordination.
condition: A plural or coordinated expression supplies the members compared.

correct.text: The twins dress alike.
The decision surprised coaches and players alike.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

statement: Unlike occurs as an adjective or preposition. Prepositional unlike can contrast predications or occur with a PP, but does not license the finite-clause complement found with like.
condition: The negative form contrasts with one of the available like constructions.

correct.text: The two proposals were unlike any we'd received before.
Unlike in the valley, it snowed before noon on the ridge.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

statement: Plain grade can invoke a contextual standard without marking a comparison. Comparative grade usually expresses term comparison, and superlative grade expresses ranking within a set in its comparative use. Better does not entail good.
condition: The interpretation distinguishes contextual standards, two terms, and ranking within a set.

correct.text: This is a small oak.
This route is worse than the other two, so it's the worst of the three.

concept: Comparative grade in two-member set comparisons
statement: Comparative grade is available for the central two-member construction. In this construction a larger set requires superlative grade. Superlatives also occur with two members, particularly when dual membership is implicit or in informal style.
condition: The of phrase explicitly identifies the members of the comparison set.
violation: The form does not satisfy the requirements of this larger-set ranking construction.

exceptions.description: Two-member sets allow comparative grade and also admit superlatives, especially in informal contexts.

correct.text: This is the sturdiest of the four frames.
That is the warmest of the three rooms.
This is the sturdier of the two frames.
This is the best of the two options.

incorrect.text: This is the sturdier of the four frames.
That is the warmer of the three rooms.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Comparative grade in two-member set comparisons
burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

That is the warmer of the three rooms. ||| That is the warmest of the three rooms.
diagnostic.learner_explanation: Use the superlative when selecting the highest-ranked member of an explicitly larger set in this construction.
diagnostic.corrected_paragraph_template: Use the superlative when selecting the highest-ranked member of an explicitly larger set in this construction.

statement: Attributive comparatives can identify a subset toward one end of a scale. An added than phrase changes the interpretation; a comparative subset need not meet the threshold associated with the plain adjective.
condition: The noun identifies a comparison class that supplies the relevant contextual scale.

correct.text: Shorter students can use the low bench.

concept: Derivational comparatives upper inner and outer
statement: Upper, inner and outer are attributive lexical forms and do not license comparative than phrases. They can contrast parts of two-member sets and form corresponding derivatives in -most.
condition: The words describe a position relative to a reference region or opposing part.

correct.text: The inner cover is removable.

concept: Temporal and anaphoric former and latter
statement: Former and latter are derivational forms without comparative than complements. Non-anaphoric former relates to an earlier reference time; non-anaphoric latter selects the later subdivision. Anaphoric former and latter select first and last, with latter sometimes used in larger sets.
condition: Prior discourse or the reference time identifies the comparison domain.

correct.text: Her former studio is now a bakery.
We could use copper or aluminum; the latter weighs less.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

statement: Superlative superiority can use -est or analytic most; analytic least marks inferiority. The construction ranks members at the relevant end of a scale.
condition: The comparison orders members along a gradable property.

correct.text: This is the shallowest pool.
This is the least expensive model.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

statement: Determiner most occurs with mass and count nouns. Least is regular with mass nouns and alternates with fewest for count plurals; the traditional preference for fewest is stronger with an overt count head than with a fused head.
condition: The noun phrase measures an amount or counts members.

correct.text: Rina used the least paint.
Rina made the fewest cuts; Jo made the least.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

concept: Clause degree adjuncts and singular nominal grading
statement: Superlative most and least can function as clause degree adjuncts. They do not parallel comparative more and less in the grading construction with of and a count singular nominal.
condition: The adjunct measures the degree of an activity or response.

correct.text: Of all of us, Tia enjoyed the exhibit most.
Tia was more of a collector than her brother.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

statement: Adjectival least means smallest or slightest and occurs predicatively or as an attributive modifier, including fused uses.
condition: Least contributes the meaning smallest or slightest in adjectival function.

correct.text: The risk is least in spring.
Even the least delay could matter.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

statement: Formal intensifying most means very. An indefinite singular article selects that reading, while adding the to an ambiguous predicative most phrase selects the superlative. Least lacks the parallel intensifier use.
condition: The surrounding determiner and predicate help determine the reading.

exceptions.description: Inflectional -est does not normally carry the intensifying reading, with conventional endearments as an exception; some formal titles use intensifying most.

correct.text: It was a most generous offer.
That was the most generous offer in the auction.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

statement: Proportional most means a majority. Superlative most compares quantities across a set and need not reach a majority. In an ambiguous context, the most or replacement by least or fewest selects set ranking.
condition: A context with multiple agents or totals can support the ranking interpretation.

correct.text: Most of the windows were open.
Kai opened the most windows.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

concept: Most as an informal reduction of almost
statement: Mostly in informal American English, reduced most can modify all, any, every, related compounds, or always.
condition: The form directly modifies the relevant quantificational or temporal expression.

correct.text: Most everyone recognized the tune.
She most always takes the early bus.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

statement: Absolute readings rank members of the set denoted within the NP. Relative readings depend on an external comparison set, such as people associated with the entities in the NP. Determinative most is overwhelmingly relative.
condition: The interpretation depends on where the comparison set is supplied.

correct.text: They rented the smallest flat in town.
Of the four cooks, Jo used the most oil.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

statement: Absolute superlatives can express possible maxima or minima. In negative environments a minimizer such as the least can mean at all. The least is a constituent with obligatory the in this minimizer use, unlike relative ranking least.
condition: The negative minimizer and relative-ranking constructions have different constituent boundaries.

correct.text: I wasn't the least worried by the warning.
Of the three hikers, I was least worried about the rain.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

statement: Incorporated superlatives occur before an NP head or are fused with it. Free superlatives occur postpositively or outside NP structure. In free superlatives the is part of the superlative phrase.
condition: The position of the superlative relative to a noun head determines its structural type.

correct.text: She chose the two cheapest lamps.
She packed the boxes most carefully.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

statement: In a modifier construction, the can be an NP determiner separate from the superlative, with a genitive or demonstrative possible. In quantity most, optional the belongs to the determiner phrase, while amount-denoting fused the most can require the.
condition: Distinguish a superlative modifying the noun from a superlative functioning as determiner.

correct.text: This is Jo's best photograph.
The most we can spend is fifty dollars.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Requires independent comparison with the Burton-Roberts structural source.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

statement: An ordinary incorporated set-ranking superlative generally requires a definite NP interpretation. A singular count head needs a determiner, and an overt numeral cannot itself be the indefinite determiner in the corresponding definite pattern. Some plural, mass and quantity examples allow omission of the without losing definiteness.
condition: The superlative is incorporated into an ordinary NP and ranks members of a set.
violation: The form does not satisfy the requirements of this incorporated ranking superlative.

exceptions.description: Lexicalized collocations can occur in indefinite NPs, and intensifying most is a distinct use.

correct.text: We chose the quietest room in the hotel.
They surveyed the two tallest buildings in town.
Several runners set personal best times.
It was a most satisfying result.

incorrect.text: We chose a quietest room in the hotel.
They surveyed two tallest buildings in town.

diagnostic.learner_explanation: Use a definite determiner in the ordinary set-ranking noun phrase.
diagnostic.corrected_paragraph_template: Use a definite determiner in the ordinary set-ranking noun phrase.

concept: Article choice in free superlative phrases
statement: Free superlatives generally allow optional the. Postpositive adjectival superlatives favor omission, and clause-level supplements such as most important of all exclude the in the illustrated construction.
condition: The superlative heads a free adjective or adverb phrase.

correct.text: Choose the route least likely to flood.
Most important of all, the well stayed clean.

statement: A free adjectival or adverbial superlative can take an integrated relative with that or a bare relative. The is obligatory in this construction, and wh relatives are excluded in the illustrated patterns.
condition: The relative depends on a free adjective or adverb superlative.
violation: The form does not satisfy the requirements of this free superlative with an integrated relative.

exceptions.description: Free superlatives without the integrated relative often allow the to be omitted. A supplementary which relative can modify a noun phrase.

correct.text: The river is the lowest it has been all summer.
The engine is running the most smoothly that it ever has.
The river is lowest in late summer.
They inspected the bridge, which was the oldest in town.

incorrect.text: The river is lowest it has been all summer.
The engine is running the most smoothly which it ever has.

statement: Possible, imaginable and related one-word dependents can precede or follow the noun in incorporated structures. A set-denoting of phrase follows the noun in that pattern and may identify entities or their associated participants.
condition: The dependent specifies an attainable extreme or gives the comparison set.

correct.text: We picked the shortest possible route.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

concept: Pre-head modifiers and rank in superlatives
statement: Very and ordinal modifiers other than first follow the in the described patterns. By far, almost, easily and similar modifiers precede it; with incorporated superlatives they are peripheral NP modifiers. Very intensifies inflectional superlatives, and ordinal ranks count from the relevant end of the scale.
condition: The placement depends on which class the pre-head modifier belongs to.

correct.text: This is the third least expensive lamp.
He made by far the fewest mistakes.

review_notes: Phase B extraction from printed text and rendered layout. Examples are original.

statement: A noncanonical information-packaging construction typically has a simpler counterpart with the same truth conditions and illocutionary meaning. The pair presents its content differently.
condition: Compare structurally distinct clauses with the same participants and proposition.

concept: Counterparts unavailable for syntactic or pragmatic reasons
statement: A noncanonical construction can be licensed even when a would-be canonical counterpart is ungrammatical or contextually infelicitous.
condition: Syntactic licensing and suitability in context must be assessed independently of semantic similarity.

correct.text: Dara was believed to have found the key.

concept: Quantifier and negation scope under repackaging
statement: Information-packaging alternants can differ in truth conditions when the change affects the relative scope of a quantifier and negation.
condition: A large number of absent members can coexist with a large number of present members.

correct.text: Many delegates weren't in the hall.

statement: Subject–dependent inversion places a verbal dependent before the verb and the subject after it. Subject–auxiliary inversion places an auxiliary before the subject.
condition: The preposed dependent and the auxiliary perform different syntactic functions.

correct.text: At the far end stood two ushers.

concept: Reordering and realignment in information packaging
statement: Preposing, postposing and subject–dependent inversion reorder clause elements. Existentials, extraposition, dislocation, clefts and passives change how semantic elements align with syntactic functions, generally adding structural material.
condition: Process terminology describes relations between constructions and their defaults.

correct.text: That proposal I rejected.
It was Dana who rejected the proposal.

statement: Information-packaging constructions can combine when their licensing conditions are compatible. Existential and extraposition constructions cannot both apply at the same clause level.
condition: Identify the clause at which each construction operates.

correct.text: It was assumed by the panel that the witness would return.

statement: Information-packaging analysis applies to entities, properties and propositions, and by extension to the expressions that represent them.
condition: Different parts of the same utterance may have different informational statuses.

concept: Discourse familiarity by mention and participation
statement: Earlier mention in the salient stretch of discourse can make a referent discourse-old, as can participation in the discourse. Real-world existence is irrelevant to discourse familiarity.
condition: Pronouns can recover an antecedent or refer directly to an interlocutor.

correct.text: I imagined a fox lived under the stairs. I called it Pepper.
I found your gloves. Do you want them?

statement: An unmentioned referent can count as discourse-old when a salient, relevant relationship connects it to something already evoked.
condition: Class membership, part–whole relations and conventional associations can support the inference.

correct.text: I tried to start the van, but the battery was dead.
I avoid most sweet pastries, but cinnamon rolls are irresistible.

statement: An open proposition can be discourse-old by inference from a prior utterance or the situation, even without explicit repetition.
condition: Recover the relation from the preceding exchange and leave the new value open.

correct.text: Can I borrow the ladder? No, but the step stool you can borrow.
Where did you put the spare keys? The front-door key I left on the hook.

statement: Discourse-old material is also addressee-old. Material introduced in the current discourse can nevertheless be addressee-old when the speaker assumes relevant shared knowledge.
condition: A shared institution or familiar participant can be identifiable on first mention.

correct.text: The moon is unusually bright tonight.
The principal has cancelled assembly, as you probably heard.

statement: The informational focus contains nuclear stress and is presented as prominent. The focus-frame is the backgrounded residue and can be represented as an open proposition.
condition: The surrounding question or context identifies which value fills the open position.

correct.text: What did Lina order? Lina ordered TEA.
Where did Lina order tea? Lina ordered tea at the STATION.

statement: Nuclear stress can occur within a larger focus constituent. Context can change the focus size without changing the stressed syllable, and a clause can contain more than one focus.
condition: Recover the focus-frame from the question and use stress to locate the focused material.

correct.text: What did she buy? She bought a tin of BEANS.
Who bought what? DANI bought a tin of BEANS.

concept: Familiar referent as a new focus value
statement: A referent already familiar to the addressee can supply new information by filling an open position in the focus-frame.
condition: Distinguish familiarity with the entity from knowing its role in the assertion.

correct.text: Did Rosa or Eli win? SHE won.
Was the package for Jo or me? It was for YOU.

statement: A focus-frame represents the background left after removing informational focus. A proposition presupposed by a factive expression can itself contain the focus.
condition: Factive presupposition and focus assignment can overlap without having the same boundaries.

statement: Constituent weight is scalar and reflects length and grammatical complexity. A heavy object can make particle-before-object order much more natural than particle-after-object order.
condition: Weight correlates with discourse novelty, while a heavy expression can refer back and a short NP can introduce a new entity.

correct.text: He folded the sheet up.

concept: Clause topic and explicit topic-shift adjuncts
statement: Clause topic is what a clause is about and is distinct from discourse topic. Some adjuncts mark an explicit topic or topic change, though most English clauses lack explicit topic marking.
condition: As for and related expressions can introduce a topic recoverable from earlier discourse.

correct.text: As for the roof, we repaired it last spring.
Speaking of travel, have you booked the ferry?

statement: Heavy and focused material tends to occur late, subjects tend to be addressee-old, and familiar information tends to precede new information.
condition: These are tendencies, and contextual suitability, syntax and stylistic variation can favor a noncanonical alternative.

statement: Complement preposing places a complement in the prenuclear position and leaves its basic VP-internal position unrealized. It is an unbounded dependency and is especially common in main declaratives, with imperative and subordinate uses also possible.
condition: The fronted element functions as a complement of the predicate.

concept: Discourse link for a preposed complement
statement: A preposed complement must connect to discourse-old information for felicity. Prior mention, a subset, a fellow member of a salient set, or an inferred scale can supply the connection. Fronted adjuncts do not share this complement-specific condition.
condition: Assess the prior discourse before judging a fronted complement.

correct.text: Do you have any drills? A cordless drill I can lend you.
Can I borrow the red scarf? It's gone, but the blue one you can borrow.

concept: Discourse-old open propositions in complement preposing
statement: Most complement preposing also has a discourse-old open proposition. Its variable may correspond to a constituent other than the preposed complement.
condition: The link supplied by the fronted expression and the familiarity of the open proposition are distinct conditions.

correct.text: Did you give out all the maps? Two of them I gave to the guide.
Where did you buy the tools? Most of them I bought at the market.
